parts.md:
The rain had followed the train all the way from Ratnagiri, sheeting sideways across paddy fields so green they looked lit from inside. Rohan Pai pressed his forehead to the window of coach C2 and traced their route on his phone's offline map. A blue dot crawled down the coast. Ahead, a dark crease in the hills marked the next tunnel.

“Two point four kilometres,” said Aaji beside him, without looking up from her knitting.

“How do you know?”

“I signalled this section for eleven years.” Her needles clicked. “Train is doing about ninety-six. You'll have a minute and a half of dark. Don't drop your phone.”

Across the aisle, a woman in a silk scarf was talking to nobody in particular, in the bright voice of someone who wanted to be overheard. She was Mrs. Lobo, an art dealer from Panjim, and on the empty seat beside her lay a long black cardboard tube.

“A Souza,” she was saying. “Well — a sketch by a student of his circle. Small. But collectors in Goa are mad for that period. I couldn't trust a courier.”

In seat 23, a heavy man in a grey safari suit — Mr. Saxena, he'd introduced himself, insurance — nodded without removing his large headphones. In 24, a girl of about nineteen with paint-stained fingers, Tanvi, was sketching the rain on the window. She glanced at the tube once, quickly, and away.

Rohan noticed the glance. He noticed, too, that Aaji had noticed him noticing. She smiled very slightly and went on knitting.

The tunnel swallowed them with a roar.

For a second the coach lights stayed on, then they flickered — the old chair cars sometimes did that on this stretch, when the power changed over — and went out. Total darkness, the kind that presses on your eyes. The roar of the wheels bounced off the tunnel walls and came back doubled.

Rohan held his phone tight. He did not switch on its torch. Afterwards he could never say why; perhaps because Aaji's hand had settled lightly on his wrist.

He heard the tea trolley first: Salim, the pantry boy, rattling past with his flask and paper cups, calling “*Chai, coffee*” into the dark as if nothing had changed. A clatter and a gasp from seat 24 — Tanvi's tin pencil box, spilling. Someone muttered *sorry, sorry*. A shuffle of feet. Then, close by, a small dry sound like a lid snapping shut: *click*.

Then daylight burst through the windows, white and wet, and the lights blinked back on.

Mrs. Lobo screamed.

The black tube lay on seat 22 with its cap off. It was empty.

Within two minutes, the Travelling Ticket Examiner, a tired man named Mr. Gawde, had arrived, followed by a Railway Protection Force constable from the next coach. Mrs. Lobo was pointing at Tanvi.

“She looked at it. I saw her. She's an art student — she knows what it's worth!”

Tanvi had gone white. “I dropped my pencils. That's all. I was picking them up.”

“In the dark? Convenient!”

Mr. Saxena had finally taken his headphones off. “Madam,” he said heavily, “if it is insured, there will be a process. Please, nobody leave the coach.”

“Nobody *can* leave the coach,” said Aaji, to Rohan, very quietly. “Listen.”

Rohan listened. The door at the end of C2, the one into the vestibule and the next coach, was opening as the constable came in. It made a long, unhappy squeal — metal on metal — that you could hear over the wheels.

“Did you hear that door during the tunnel?” Aaji asked.

Rohan thought hard. Trolley. Pencils. *Sorry, sorry.* Click.

“No.”

“Then the painting is still in this coach,” said Aaji, and she went back to her knitting, as though she had remarked on the weather.

The constable searched everyone's bags. It took forty minutes and found nothing but snacks, novels and an alarming number of chargers. Tanvi's sketchbook was turned page by page; it was full of rain, and boats, and once, Rohan saw, a quick little drawing of Aaji knitting, which made him like Tanvi more.

The painting was not in any bag. It was not under any seat. It was not in the toilet, the dustbin or the overhead racks, which the constable swept with his torch.

“Thrown out of a window?” said Mr. Gawde.

“These windows don't open,” said Rohan. “It's a chair car. They're sealed.”

“Then where?”

Rohan took out his napkin and drew the coach: seats 21 to 26, the aisle, the luggage rack, the trolley's path. He drew arrows for every sound. *Trolley passing 22. Pencils at 24. Click near the rack — above 23?*

“A rolled canvas,” he said slowly, “is long and thin. Like a tube. Or a pole. Or—”

He stopped, because Salim the pantry boy was coming back up the aisle with his trolley, and on the trolley, as on every trip, stood a tall steel flask of tea.

“Salim,” said Aaji pleasantly. “One chai, please.”

Salim poured. The tea came out of the flask hot and sweet, a perfectly ordinary stream. Rohan's heart sank. Not the flask, then.

Aaji sipped. “You went past seat 22 in the tunnel?”

“Yes, Aaji. I always go through. Even in the dark. People want tea.” He grinned. “Twelve years on this train.”

“Did anybody touch your trolley?”

Salim thought. “Somebody bumped. Near the pencil-box girl. I thought it was her, bending down.”

Rohan looked at the trolley properly for the first time. It was a battered steel cart with two shelves. On the bottom shelf, half-hidden by a crate of biscuits, was a long folded rain umbrella — the sort with a hollow metal shaft and a curved wooden handle — strapped under the shelf with a rubber band.

“Is that yours?” Rohan asked.

Salim looked down. His face changed. “No,” he said. “I don't — no. I never saw that before.”

The constable unfolded the umbrella. Nothing. He shook it. Nothing.

But Aaji held out her hand, and he gave it to her, a little puzzled. She turned the curved wooden handle. It unscrewed. Inside the hollow shaft, rolled tight as a cigar, was a small canvas.

Mrs. Lobo gave a cry and reached for it.

“One moment,” said Aaji. She held the shaft up to the window. “The question is not *where*. The question is *who*. Somebody put this umbrella on Salim's trolley in the dark, because they knew the trolley would roll on to the pantry car at the next station and they could collect it there, far from this coach, with nobody searching them.”

“So Salim was the delivery boy,” Rohan said, “without knowing.”

“Exactly.”

“But the click,” Rohan said. “The click was near the luggage rack. Above 23.”

Everyone looked at Mr. Saxena, who had put his headphones back on and was gazing out of the window with great concentration.

“I heard nothing,” said Mr. Saxena, when the constable tapped him. “I had music on.”

“What music?” asked Aaji.

“Old Hindi songs. Rafi.”

“Lovely. May I?” Before he could object she lifted one earcup gently to her own ear. She listened, and handed it back. “Silent,” she said. “Your headphones are not connected to anything. The wire ends in your pocket.”

Saxena's face went a slow brick red.

Rohan's mind was racing. “The click — that was the umbrella handle screwing shut, wasn't it? You stood up in the dark, took the canvas from the tube on 22, rolled it into the shaft, screwed the handle and slipped it under the trolley shelf when Salim passed. You wore headphones the whole trip so nobody would talk to you, and so later you could say you heard nothing.”

“And you're an insurance agent,” said Aaji, “so you knew that Mrs. Lobo would make a claim — and that you could sell the painting quietly and nobody would look too hard at a man who'd been listening to Rafi.”

“You can't prove the click was me,” Saxena muttered.

“No,” Aaji agreed. “But the umbrella can. It is still wet from the platform at Ratnagiri. Everyone else in this coach boarded at Mumbai, under a dry sky, before the rain began. You were the only passenger who got on at Ratnagiri.”

At Madgaon, the RPF were waiting on the platform. Mr. Saxena — whose real name, it turned out, was not Saxena at all, and who was not an insurance agent either — went quietly.

Mrs. Lobo held the little canvas against her chest and, to everyone's surprise, burst into tears. Then she turned to Tanvi.

“I accused you,” she said. “I'm sorry. I was frightened, and you were young, and you looked at it.”

“I looked because it's beautiful,” said Tanvi. “I've only ever seen that style in books.”

Mrs. Lobo unrolled the canvas a few inches, very carefully, and let Tanvi look properly: a few bold black lines of a fisherman, and a smear of blue that might have been the sea.

Salim got a fifty-rupee tip from the TTE and a hundred from Mrs. Lobo, and spent the next hour telling the whole pantry car the story, getting the details more wrong each time.

On the platform, Rohan folded his napkin map and put it in his pocket. “How did you know he got on at Ratnagiri?” he asked Aaji.

“I watched who boarded,” she said. “Old habit. When you have spent your life keeping trains from running into each other, you learn to notice who is where, and when.”

She tucked her knitting into her bag. “Also,” she added, “Rafi would never be that quiet.”

summary: A painting is stolen from an AC chair-car coach during a 90-second tunnel blackout on the Konkan line.

The squealing vestibule door was never heard, so the painting never left the coach.

Mr. Saxena's headphones were unplugged — he had been listening all along.
The wet umbrella proved its owner boarded at rainy Ratnagiri; only Saxena had.

rd-stories-ladakh-mirror.title: The Mirror on Stok Ridge
rd-stories-ladakh-mirror.subtitle: No phone signal, a sprained ankle, a snowstorm coming — and one small mirror. A Ladakh mountain adventure.

sections.md:
**Ladakh** is a high, cold desert in the far north of India, where mountains rise above 6,000 metres and the air is so thin that visitors must rest a day or two before they walk anywhere. The sky is a blue you have never seen. The sun is fierce, even when the wind is freezing.

**Anaya** (11) has come from Chennai to spend the summer with her uncle **Tsering**, a mountain guide, and his son **Dorje** (10). She has never seen snow. She has never been colder than an air-conditioned cinema.

On the fifth day of a short trek, Tsering slips on loose rock — and the two children have to get help with no phone signal at all.

The characters are fictional. The science — altitude, sunlight, signalling — is real.

sections.h: How a mirror becomes a signal
sections.md:
A flat mirror reflects light following a simple rule: **the angle the light comes in at equals the angle it bounces out at**. On a sunny day, a small mirror can throw a flash of bright sunlight across a valley. Pilots and rescue teams have seen mirror flashes from tens of kilometres away in clear air.

To aim it, you hold up two fingers in a V towards your target, and tilt the mirror until the bright spot of reflected light falls on your fingers. Then the flash is travelling towards the target.

A steady glint can look like sunlight on a car window. A **pattern** of flashes looks like a message. The international distress pattern is **three** signals in a row, repeated — three flashes, three whistles, three fires. In Morse code, **SOS** is ··· — — — ··· (three short, three long, three short).

**Did you know?** In Ladakh, the air is thin and dry, so there is much less haze than in cities. That is why the mountains look so sharp — and why a flash travels so far.

sections.h: Altitude: why the mountains are hard
sections.md:
At sea level, like in Chennai, the air pressing on you is thick. At about 3,500 m (Leh) the air pressure is roughly two-thirds of sea level, so each breath carries less oxygen. At 4,500 m it is even less — a bit over half.

That's why trekkers **acclimatise** — rest, drink water and climb slowly so the body can adjust. Headaches, breathlessness and tiredness are warning signs; going *down* is the best cure.

The Sun is also stronger at height, because there is less air to filter ultraviolet light. Sunglasses and sunscreen are essential — even when it's freezing.

parts.md:
The first thing Anaya noticed about Ladakh was that she couldn't breathe.

Not properly, anyway. She walked down the aeroplane steps at Leh airport, took three steps across the tarmac, and felt as if she'd climbed four floors of stairs. Her head buzzed. The sky above her was an impossible blue, deeper than any colour she had seen in Chennai, and the mountains all around were bare and brown and gold, with white snow on their tops like icing.

"Breathe slowly," said Uncle Tsering, taking her bag. He was a mountain guide, broad and smiling, with a face browned by the sun. "Nobody walks fast on their first day in Leh. Not even me."

His son Dorje was ten and had been born here. He looked at Anaya's pink trainers, her thin jacket and her phone and said, "You'll need a hat."

For two days Anaya did nothing but rest, drink lemon-ginger tea, eat thukpa (noodle soup so hot it made her nose run) and look out of the window at the mountains. Uncle Tsering said this was called *acclimatising*: giving your body time to get used to the thin air.

By the third day she could walk around the old town without puffing. By the fourth, Dorje had taught her to say *julley* — the Ladakhi greeting that means hello, goodbye, please and thank you all at once.

And on the fifth day, they left for the mountains.

It was only a short trek — three days up a valley to a high camp below Stok Ridge, then back down. Uncle Tsering had done it a hundred times. They carried tents, a little gas stove, food, water bottles, warm clothes, and a small first-aid kit.

And in the front pocket of Uncle Tsering's rucksack, though nobody thought about it at the time, a small round steel mirror he used for shaving.

The valley was like walking inside a giant's sandpit. Cliffs of red and purple and green rock rose on either side. A river rushed down the middle, grey with melted glacier ice. Prayer flags fluttered on a pile of stones, red, yellow, green, white and blue, sending their prayers out on the wind.

They saw a marmot — a fat, furry, golden animal like an enormous guinea pig — sitting up outside its burrow and whistling at them. They saw a lammergeier, a huge bearded vulture, gliding high above on wings almost three metres across. Dorje spotted blue sheep (which were not blue at all, but grey) on a cliff so steep it seemed impossible anything could stand on it.

Anaya was tired, but happy. Her phone had lost signal on the first morning, and after an hour of checking it every five minutes she'd stopped noticing.

On the second evening, at the high camp, it was so cold that her water bottle froze solid inside the tent. She lay in her sleeping bag wearing every piece of clothing she owned and listened to the wind tugging at the tent.

"Can I ask you something?" she whispered to Dorje.

"Mm."

"What happens if something goes wrong up here? There's no signal. No road. No nothing."

Dorje was quiet for a moment. "Abba says the mountains don't care about phones. You have to look after yourself, and look after each other."

It didn't make Anaya feel better at all.

The next morning was perfect. Not a cloud. The sun lit up the snow peaks pink, then gold, then dazzling white. Uncle Tsering said they'd walk up the ridge for an hour to see the view, then pack up camp and head down.

The view was worth every gasping step. From the top of the ridge, the whole world spread out: range after range of mountains, the green ribbon of the Indus valley far below, and a tiny cluster of white houses and green fields that Uncle Tsering said was the village of Stok, where his cousin lived.

"That's a long way," said Anaya.

"Twelve kilometres as the eagle flies," said Uncle Tsering. "A day's walk for us."

On the way back down, it happened.

They were crossing a slope of loose, broken stones — scree, Uncle Tsering called it — and he was in front, testing each step. A stone rolled under his boot. He slid, twisted, and went down hard on one knee with a shout.

When he tried to stand, his face went grey. His right ankle would not hold him.

"Sprained," he said through his teeth. "Badly. Maybe broken." He tried to smile. "Well. This is inconvenient."

Anaya's legs felt like water. Dorje went very still.

They helped him — slowly, painfully — back to the camp. It took two hours to cover what should have been twenty minutes. By the time he was lying in the tent with his boot off and his ankle swollen like a balloon, it was nearly noon.

And on the western horizon, behind the peaks, a long line of grey cloud was creeping up the sky.

"Snow," said Uncle Tsering, looking at the clouds through the tent door. "Tonight, maybe tomorrow morning." He was quiet, thinking. "I can't walk down. Not on this ankle. Not for days."

"Then I'll go," said Dorje at once. "I'll run down to Stok and get help."

"No." Uncle Tsering's voice was suddenly sharp. "Twelve kilometres, alone, over the pass, with a storm coming? No. Never split up in the mountains. That's how you lose two people instead of one."

Anaya pulled out her phone. No signal. Of course. She walked to the edge of the camp and held it up high. Nothing. She climbed onto a boulder. Nothing.

She stared down at the tiny village, far below in the sunshine. There were people there. Real people, with cars and phones and doctors. They just couldn't *see* them.

*They just couldn't see them.*

Anaya stood on the boulder, very still, her heart beating faster.

She was thinking about a science lesson. Mrs Krishnan's class, Chennai, last winter. The chapter on light. *A plane mirror reflects light. The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection.* Mrs Krishnan had taken them out into the school courtyard with little mirrors and they had flashed sunlight onto the walls, onto each other's faces, onto the window of the staff room until the Principal came out and told them to stop.

She remembered how *bright* that spot of light had been. Bright enough to make the Principal squint, all the way across the courtyard.

"Uncle," she said, jumping off the boulder. "Do you have a mirror?"

The shaving mirror was round, about the size of a biscuit, made of polished steel with a little hole at the top for hanging it on a nail.

Anaya held it up to the sun. A dazzling spot of light leapt onto the tent, so bright that Dorje yelped and shielded his eyes.

"Can people in Stok see that?" he asked.

"I don't know," said Anaya honestly. "But the air here is so clear. And it's so sunny. And there's nothing else up here that shines."

Uncle Tsering, propped up on his rucksack, was looking at her with a strange expression. "My cousin Padma's house is the one with the green roof, at the top of the village. She's always out in the fields at this time of year." He paused. "It might work. If you can aim it."

That was the hard part. Anaya could see the village, but it was tiny. How could she be sure the flash was going there and not just splashing around the mountains?

Then she remembered something else. Not from Mrs Krishnan this time — from a survival show she'd watched on TV with her father.

She stretched out her left arm towards the village and made a V with two fingers, so the green roof sat right in the gap between them. Then, with her right hand, she held the mirror near her cheek and tilted it, slowly, until the bright spot of reflected light landed on her own two fingers.

"If the light hits my fingers," she explained, "and my fingers are pointing at the village, then the light is going to the village too."

Dorje stared at her. "Where did you learn that?"

"Mrs Krishnan," said Anaya. "And television."

She flashed. And flashed. And flashed.

"Wait," said Uncle Tsering after a few minutes. "If you just shine it, Padma will think it's the sun on a car window or a tin roof. You need to make it look like a *message*."

"Like Morse code?"

"Like three," he said. "In the mountains, three of anything means help. Three whistles. Three shouts. Three fires. Do it in threes."

Anaya knew SOS from a book: *dot-dot-dot, dash-dash-dash, dot-dot-dot*. She worked out a system with Dorje. She would hold the mirror steady on her V-fingers. Dorje would hold his flat hand in front of the mirror to block it, then move his hand away — quickly for a short flash, slowly for a long one.

Short, short, short.

Long, long, long.

Short, short, short.

Pause. Count to ten. Again.

They did it for half an hour. Then an hour. Anaya's arm ached so much she had to swap hands. Dorje started counting out loud in Ladakhi to keep the rhythm. The sun was hot on their faces even though the wind was icy.

And the line of grey cloud crept higher. Soon it would reach the sun. And then there would be no light to flash at all.

"It's not working," whispered Dorje.

"Keep going," said Anaya, though she was starting to think the same thing.

Short, short, short. Long, long, long. Short, short, short.

Then, far below, in the little cluster of houses — so tiny that at first she thought she had imagined it — something winked back.

One. Two. Three.

"THEY SAW!" screamed Dorje, so loudly that a marmot somewhere whistled in alarm. "Abba! Abba! They flashed back!"

Far below, the little light winked again — three times, then three times again. Someone in Stok had a mirror too, or a car window they were tilting, and they were saying: *We see you.*

Uncle Tsering put his face in his hands. When he looked up, his eyes were wet. "Good girl," he said quietly. "Good, clever girl."

The clouds swallowed the sun twenty minutes later. The wind rose. The first fine, dry flakes of snow began to fall, swirling around the tent. Anaya and Dorje crawled inside and huddled close to Uncle Tsering, and the three of them shared the last packet of biscuits and the gas stove's little blue flame.

Four hours later, just before dark, they heard voices.

Three men from Stok — Padma's husband, her eldest son, and a soldier from the army post near the village — came up the trail through the snow, carrying a stretcher made of poles and canvas, a flask of hot butter tea and a radio.

"Padma saw your flashes from the field," said Padma's husband, crouching beside Uncle Tsering. "She said, 'Nobody shines a tin roof in threes.' She sent us up straight away and called the army post."

The soldier spoke into his radio. The next morning, when the snow had passed and the sky was clear again, a helicopter came clattering up the valley and lifted Uncle Tsering to the hospital in Leh.

The ankle was broken, as it turned out — a clean break, which the doctor in Leh said would heal perfectly in eight weeks, "as long as he doesn't try to climb anything". Uncle Tsering grumbled about this, but not very much.

Anaya spent the rest of her summer in Ladakh, and it was the best summer of her life. She learned to make momos with Dorje's mother, pinching the edges into little pleats. She went to a festival at a monastery where monks danced in huge painted masks. She went to Stok to meet Padma, a small cheerful woman with a red scarf and a laugh like a bell, who gave her a hug and a jar of apricot jam.

"You know," said Padma, "when I first saw your light, I thought it was nothing. Then I saw it again. And again. And I thought — *that light is counting*."

On her last day, Uncle Tsering, now on crutches, gave Anaya a present wrapped in a white silk scarf — a *khatak*, the scarf Ladakhis give to honour guests.

Inside was the round steel shaving mirror.

"I'll buy a new one," he said. "This one belongs to you now. Every guide should carry one. And every guide should know how to use it."

Back in Chennai, in September, Mrs Krishnan asked the class to write an essay called *What I Did This Summer*.

Anaya wrote eleven pages. She called it *Angle of Incidence*.

Mrs Krishnan gave it full marks, and wrote at the bottom in red ink: *I always said this chapter would be useful one day.*

rd-stories-language-of-rain.title: The Language of Rain
rd-stories-language-of-rain.subtitle: A young coder returns to Kerala when her father loses his words — and finds them in his old notebooks.

sections.md:
This is a **literary story**: less about *what happens* than about how people change. There is no villain and no puzzle. Read it the way you would listen to someone telling you about their family late at night.

**Anjali**, twenty-six, writes software in Bengaluru. Her father **Madhavan**, a retired Malayalam schoolteacher in a village near Kottayam, has a stroke and develops **aphasia** — difficulty finding and producing words. She goes home for two weeks and stays for a monsoon.

The story uses short scenes, shifts in time, and images that return — rain, a red notebook, a mango tree — the way memory works.

sections.md:
Notice how the writer builds meaning:

- **Motifs.** Rain appears in every part, but its meaning shifts — from inconvenience, to fear, to comfort.
- **Showing, not telling.** We are never told Anjali feels guilty; we see her answer work calls in the bathroom.
- **Language as theme.** A story about a man losing words is told partly through the words he once wrote.
- **Open ending.** Nothing is 'fixed'. Something is understood.

sections.md:
**Aphasia** is a language disorder, often caused by stroke, that affects speaking, understanding, reading or writing. It does **not** usually affect intelligence: a person may know exactly what they mean and be unable to say it. Speech and language therapists help with exercises, picture boards and other communication aids. Recovery varies a great deal from person to person.

*This is general information, not medical advice — families should follow the guidance of the treating doctor and therapist.*

check.q: Which statement about aphasia is accurate?
options: It always means a person cannot think clearly
It is a language disorder that need not affect intelligence
It is cured in a week
check.why: Aphasia disrupts language processing, but many people with it keep their intelligence and understanding of the world.

parts.md:
The call came at 2:40 in the afternoon, during a sprint review. Anjali saw *Amma* on the screen and sent it to voicemail, because her mother called every day at odd hours to ask whether she had eaten. It rang again. Then her cousin Biju. Then Amma again.

She stepped out of the glass meeting room into the corridor where the pantry smelled of burnt filter coffee and answered, and her mother said, “Achan—” and then nothing, just breathing, and in the background a hospital announcement in Malayalam that Anjali understood before her mother found the words.

She was on the night bus by nine. It was the second week of June, and somewhere past Salem the monsoon met the bus head-on. Rain thrashed the windows. The driver slowed to a crawl. Anjali sat with her laptop open on her knees, answering messages from her manager — *of course, take the time you need, just make sure the release notes are handed over* — and watched the wipers fail against the water.

She told herself: two weeks. She had done the arithmetic of leave on her phone. Two weeks was enough to see him stable, to talk to doctors, to arrange a home nurse. She was good at arranging. It was the thing she did best.

Outside, Kerala began, first as a smell — wet laterite, coconut husk, diesel — and then as a green so dense that the bus seemed to be travelling through the inside of a leaf.

Achan was sitting up in the hospital bed when she arrived, which was more than she had prepared herself for. He was thinner. The right side of his face had slipped, very slightly, like a picture hung a little crooked. When he saw her, his eyes filled.

He opened his mouth and said, carefully, “*Kudam*.”

Pot.

Anjali looked at her mother. Her mother looked at the floor.

“He means you,” Amma said quietly. “He keeps saying the wrong word. The doctor says the words are all still in there. They come out — sideways.”

Achan tried again. His good hand gripped the sheet. “*Kudam. Kudam.*” Then, furious, frightened, he shook his head and hit the mattress, once, and turned his face to the wall.

This was the man who had taught Malayalam grammar to three generations of children in the government school two kilometres down the road. Who corrected the pronunciation of newsreaders on television. Who had once, when she was nine, made her rewrite a birthday card to her grandmother four times because she had misused a single case ending.

*Aphasia*, the neurologist said in English, in the corridor, as if English were gentler. *Expressive, mostly. Comprehension seems largely intact. He understands you. He can't always answer. Therapy will help. It will be slow.*

Anjali typed it all into her phone. Then she went to the hospital bathroom and joined a call about a database migration, and spoke very calmly for twenty minutes, and did not cry until afterwards.

They brought him home after nine days. The house had not changed: red-oxide floors cool underfoot, the long veranda, the wooden easy-chair with its cane seat worn into the shape of him, the mango tree leaning over the well. Rain fell, stopped, fell again. The power went out each afternoon at four and came back at six.

Anjali set up her laptop on the dining table, the only place with a signal, and worked in two time zones: Bengaluru's, which was all deadlines, and the house's, which was all waiting. The speech therapist came twice a week, a brisk young woman named Remya who held up picture cards — *cup, chair, banana, bus* — and waited, smiling, while Achan's mouth worked.

Sometimes the word came. Sometimes another word came. Sometimes nothing came and his face went grey with effort.

Anjali found she could not watch. She would take her laptop to the veranda, or find something urgent to arrange: a ramp for the back step, a commode chair, a pharmacy that delivered. Amma watched her doing it and said nothing, which in Amma's language meant a great deal.

One night, unable to sleep, Anjali went into her father's study looking for a charger. The room smelled of him — camphor, old paper, the Cuticura powder he had used for forty years. On the lowest shelf, behind dictionaries, was a stack of red school notebooks, the cheap kind with multiplication tables printed on the back.

She almost threw them in the box marked *raddi* for the paper man. Then she opened one.

It was a diary, of sorts. Not a daily one. Entries were dated months apart, sometimes years. They were in her father's Malayalam handwriting — upright, round, every letter perfectly formed, the hand of a man who wrote on blackboards.

*14 June 1998. The rains came today. Anjali, three years old, ran onto the veranda and stood with her arms out and shouted 'mazha, mazha' at the sky as if she had invented it. I have taught the word to six hundred children. None of them said it as well.*

She turned the page.

*2 March 2004. She asked me today why I do not speak English at home. I told her a language is a house. You can visit other houses. But you should not forget the way back to your own.*

And later, in a hand slightly shakier:

*30 July 2017. She has gone to Bengaluru. The house is very quiet. Her mother pretends she is not crying. I pretend I am reading. We are both bad at pretending.*

Anjali sat on the floor of the study with the notebook in her lap while the rain hammered the tiles overhead, and read until the window went grey with dawn. Her father had never said any of it. Not one word. He had written it all down, in the language he had taught her, and put it behind the dictionaries where no one would look.

She realised she had not spoken Malayalam to him — not properly, not in whole sentences — in about four years.

In the morning she did not open her work laptop. She opened her personal one.

She had an idea, half-formed, the kind she usually had at work and turned into a ticket. Remya used picture cards. Cards were slow and fixed. But Achan's words weren't gone — they were *sideways*. What if the cards could be sorted the way his mind seemed to be sorting them now? What if, when he said *kudam*, she could see what else lived near *kudam* in his head?

She built a simple board on a tablet over three nights. Big tiles, each with a picture and a word in Malayalam script. When he pressed one, the tablet spoke the word aloud. She recorded the voice herself, in Malayalam, her pronunciation a little rusty. Twice she had to look up words she had forgotten.

Then she added something else. On the first page, she put six tiles she had chosen from the red notebooks. *Mazha* — rain. *Veedu* — house. *Mangha* — mango. *Amma*. *Anjali*. And one more, the one that had made her cry at four in the morning: *vazhi* — the way, the path.

She brought it to him on the veranda at five o'clock, in the gap between two showers, when the light turned green and the frogs started.

“Achan,” she said, in Malayalam, slowly. “I made something. Can I show you?”

He looked at the tablet with suspicion. He had always disliked her phone — *that box that eats your face*, he called it. But he let her put it on his knee.

She pressed the first tile. Her own voice came out, shy and slightly off-key: *Mazha*.

Achan stared at the tile. At the little picture of rain. Then he looked out at the actual rain beginning again across the paddy beyond the well, silver over green, and his lips moved.

“*Mazha*,” he said.

Clearly. Correctly. The right word in the right place, for the first time in a month.

Amma, in the doorway, put her hand over her mouth.

He pressed *Anjali*. The tablet said her name in her own voice. He looked at her, and his face did the crooked, half-paralysed thing it did now that was nonetheless, unmistakably, a smile.

“*Kudam*,” he said, tapping her hand. And then — slowly, with immense effort, his jaw working — “*Al-la*. *Anjali*.”

*Not pot. Anjali.*

She laughed. She cried. She did both at the same time, which she had not known people really did outside films, and her father patted her hand with his good one, exactly as he had done when she fell off her bicycle at seven, and said nothing, because for once nothing needed saying.

Two weeks became four. She spoke to her manager, then to HR, and arranged — because she was good at arranging — to work remotely through the end of the monsoon. Her manager was kinder than she had expected. Somebody in her team, she learned, had done the same thing for a mother in Patna the year before.

The routine changed. In the mornings she worked at the dining table, and when the power cut out at four, she closed the laptop without guilt. She sat with Achan on the veranda and they worked through the board. She added tiles every evening — words he asked for by pointing, words from the notebooks, words from his old school textbooks that were still on the top shelf. Remya, the therapist, was delighted and slightly professionally jealous, and asked whether she could use the idea with other patients. Anjali sent her the files.

Some days were bad. Some days Achan was exhausted and angry and threw the tablet onto the cushion and would not look at either of them. Some days the right word refused to come and the wrong one came again and again, like a stuck key. On those days they just sat. The rain did the talking.

She started reading the red notebooks to him aloud. At first he looked embarrassed, then fierce, then — when she reached the entry about her standing on the veranda shouting at the sky — he closed his eyes, and his good hand moved on the arm of the chair, conducting something only he could hear.

On the last evening of September, the rains began to soften — the long steady downpours of July giving way to short bright showers that came and went like visitors. The paddy had turned from green to gold. The mango tree dripped.

Anjali's bag was packed by the door. She was going back to Bengaluru for a month, then home again for Onam next year, and in between, Biju and a nurse and Remya and Amma, and a video call every evening at six when the power came back.

Achan was in his easy-chair. He had the tablet on his knee, but he wasn't using it. He was looking at her.

He worked his mouth for a long time. She waited. She had learned to wait.

“*Vazhi*,” he said at last.

The way. The path.

She knelt by the chair. “*Ariyaam*, Achan,” she said. I know. “I won't forget the way back.”

He shook his head, impatient, the old schoolteacher dissatisfied with a student's answer. He lifted his good hand and tapped her chest, just over her heart, twice. Then he pointed past her, out at the rain, at the road, at the whole wide wet world beyond the gate.

It took her a moment to understand. He wasn't telling her to come back.

He was telling her that she could go — that the way home was something she carried, not something she had to stand on.

Outside, it began to rain again, lightly, as if somebody had remembered one more thing to say.

Her father, a Malayalam teacher, develops aphasia: his words come out 'sideways'.
She first copes by arranging things and hiding in work.
She discovers his red notebooks — a hidden diary of love he never spoke aloud.
She builds a Malayalam word board on a tablet, recording the words in her own voice.
The word 'mazha' (rain) is his first clear word in a month.
She learns to wait, to sit with silence, and to read his notebooks to him.
She arranges remote work and stays through the monsoon.
His final word, 'vazhi' (the way), tells her home is something she carries.

rd-stories-monkey-crocodile.title: The Monkey and the Crocodile
rd-stories-monkey-crocodile.subtitle: A Panchatantra tale retold: a friendship built on rose-apples, a dangerous ride across the river, and the fastest thinking in the forest.

sections.md:
More than two thousand years ago — scholars usually place it somewhere between about 300 BCE and 300 CE, though nobody knows exactly — a collection of animal stories was put together in Sanskrit. It was called the **Panchatantra**, meaning *five books* or *five principles*.

According to the frame story, a king was worried because his three sons were, frankly, not very bright. A wise teacher named **Vishnu Sharma** promised to make them wise in six months — not with lectures, but with **stories**. Each story had animals who were clever or foolish, loyal or greedy, and each taught a lesson about life and how to deal with people.

The Panchatantra travelled the world. It was translated into Persian, Arabic, and many European languages, and its tales turned up in collections across Asia and Europe.

This is a **retelling in our own words** of one of its most famous stories, from the fourth book, which is about *losing what you have gained*.

Translated into Middle Persian (Pahlavi)

sections.md:
The moral usually given is:

> *Presence of mind can save you when strength cannot.*

But there are others hidden inside:

- **Think before you trust** someone who is acting strangely, even a friend.
- **Don't let others push you into betraying a friend.** The crocodile listens to his wife's greed instead of his own heart.
- **Honesty matters.** Once the crocodile has lied, the friendship can never be the same.
- **A calm mind is a sharp mind.** The monkey is terrified — and still thinks.

**Did you know?** Rose-apples (*jamun* in some retellings, *jambu* in older ones) are real fruit trees that grow along Indian riverbanks.

check.q: What saved the monkey in the middle of the river?
options: Quick thinking and a clever story
check.why: The monkey could not fight or swim, so he invented a story about leaving his heart in the tree, which made the crocodile carry him back to safety.

parts.md:
On the bank of a wide, slow river, there grew a rose-apple tree.

It was the finest tree for miles. Its branches spread out over the water like a green umbrella, and in summer it was so heavy with fruit — pink and pale green, crisp and sweet and juicy — that the branches dipped almost into the river.

In this tree lived a monkey. His name was **Rakta-mukha**, which means *red-face*, because his face was the colour of a ripe fruit. He was not the biggest monkey in the forest, nor the strongest, but he was cheerful and kind, and he had the best tree in the world all to himself.

One hot afternoon, a long, knobbly shape came gliding up the river. It slid out onto the muddy bank under the tree and lay there in the shade, its mouth open, panting in the heat.

It was a crocodile. His name was **Karala-mukha** — *fearsome-face* — though at that moment he didn't look very fearsome at all. He looked tired and hot and rather hungry.

The monkey looked down from his branch. Monkeys and crocodiles were not usually friends. But this crocodile was a guest under his tree, and in the old days, people said: *a guest is like a god*. You do not turn a guest away.

"Hello, friend!" called Rakta-mukha. "You look as if you've come a long way. Would you like something to eat?"

The crocodile blinked his great yellow eyes in surprise. "That's... very kind."

The monkey picked the ripest, juiciest rose-apples and dropped them, one by one, *plop, plop, plop*, right into the crocodile's open mouth.

The crocodile had never tasted anything like it. He chewed slowly, his eyes half closed. Sweet juice ran down his long jaw.

"More?" asked the monkey, laughing.

"If you don't mind," said the crocodile.

After that, Karala-mukha came back the next day, and the next, and the next. Every afternoon, he would slide out of the water and lie under the rose-apple tree, and every afternoon the monkey would come down to the lowest branch, and they would talk.

They talked about everything. The crocodile told stories of the river — of deep pools where great fish lived, of fishermen and their nets, of the floods in the rainy season when the whole world turned to water. The monkey told stories of the forest — of tigers and peacocks, of the elephant herd that came through every spring, of the funny little squirrels who always tried to steal his fruit.

The crocodile laughed at the monkey's jokes. The monkey listened to the crocodile's worries. Little by little, they became the best of friends.

One evening, as the sun was setting, the crocodile said, a little shyly: "Friend, I have a wife at home, on the other side of the river. She lives on an island in the middle of the water. May I take her some of your rose-apples?"

"Of course!" said the monkey at once. "Take as many as you like. A friend's wife is family."

And he filled the crocodile's mouth with the best fruit on the tree, and waved goodbye as Karala-mukha swam away into the dusk.

The crocodile's wife was waiting for him on their island, as she did every evening, cross that he was late again.

"Where have you *been*?" she said. "Every day you come home later and later."

"I've brought you something," said the crocodile, and gave her the rose-apples.

She ate one. Then another. Then all of them. Her eyes grew wide. "Where did you get these? They're delicious!"

So the crocodile told her all about his friend the monkey, and the rose-apple tree, and their long afternoons talking under its branches.

His wife listened very carefully. When he finished, she was quiet for a long while. Then she said, slowly:

"This monkey eats these sweet rose-apples every single day. Every single day, for years and years. Just think how sweet his *heart* must be."

The crocodile felt something cold go down his spine. "What do you mean?"

"I mean," said his wife, "that I want to eat the monkey's heart. It must be the sweetest thing in the whole world."

"But — he's my *friend*!" said the crocodile. "He has been kind to me. He gave you this fruit!"

His wife turned her back on him. "So you care more about a monkey than about your own wife. I see. If you won't bring me his heart, I won't eat anything at all. I'll starve myself. And it will be *your* fault."

And she lay down and refused to eat, and refused to speak, for a whole day, and then another.

The crocodile was miserable.

He loved his wife. He didn't want her to be unhappy, and he certainly didn't want her to starve. But he loved his friend, too. He lay in the water and thought, and thought, and every thought went round in a circle and came back to the same place.

On the third day, his wife still had not eaten. She was very weak.

And so, with a heavy heart, the crocodile decided. He would betray his friend.

*It's not right*, said a little voice inside him. But he swam across the river anyway.

The monkey was waiting on his branch. "Friend! Where have you been? I was worried. I saved you the best fruit!"

The crocodile could not look him in the eye. "My wife," he said, "wants to meet you. She says you have been so kind to us, she must thank you herself. She has prepared a feast. Will you come to our home for dinner?"

The monkey was delighted. "Of course! But — your home is on an island in the middle of the river. I can't swim."

"Climb on my back," said the crocodile. "I'll carry you."

So the monkey, who trusted his friend completely, jumped down from the lowest branch and landed on the crocodile's broad, bumpy back. He held on tightly. And the crocodile pushed off from the bank and swam out into the deep, dark river.

At first, the monkey loved it. The water rushed past. The wind blew through his fur. The bank grew smaller behind them, and the island grew bigger ahead.

But when they reached the very middle of the river — where the water was deepest and the current was strongest, and the banks on both sides were far, far away — the crocodile slowed down.

And then, little by little, he began to sink.

The water rose over his back. It came up to the monkey's feet, then his knees.

"Friend!" cried the monkey. "You're going under! I'll drown!"

The crocodile felt so guilty that the truth burst out of him. He was too far from shore now; the monkey couldn't escape. What did it matter if he knew?

"I'm sorry," said Karala-mukha. "I'm so sorry. There is no feast. My wife wants to eat your heart. She says it must be sweet from all the rose-apples. She says she'll starve unless I bring it to her. I'm taking you to her so that she can — so that —"

He couldn't finish.

The monkey's whole body went cold. He was in the middle of a deep river, on the back of a crocodile, and he could not swim. He could not fight. He could not run.

All he could do was *think*.

*Stay calm*, he told himself. *A frightened mind is a foolish mind. Think, Rakta-mukha. Think!*

The monkey took a deep breath. When he spoke, his voice was surprisingly cheerful.

"Oh, my dear friend! Why didn't you *tell* me before?"

The crocodile was so surprised he stopped sinking. "What?"

"If your wife wanted my heart," said the monkey, "I'd have been honoured to give it to her! But you see, there's a problem." He shook his head sadly. "We monkeys don't carry our hearts around with us. They're far too precious. We might drop them while jumping from branch to branch! So we always keep them safe, high up in our trees. My heart is hanging on the top branch of the rose-apple tree, right this minute."

The crocodile thought about this. He was not a very quick thinker.

"Really?" he said.

"Of course," said the monkey. "Everyone knows that. If you'd told me on the bank, I'd have brought it with me. Now we'll have to go all the way back to fetch it. Your poor wife will have to wait even longer."

The crocodile felt terrible about his wife waiting. He turned round at once. "Then we'll go back — quickly! You get your heart, and I'll bring you straight back here."

"Excellent idea," said the monkey. "Swim fast!"

And the crocodile rose up out of the water and swam as fast as he could, back across the river, towards the rose-apple tree.

The moment the crocodile's nose touched the muddy bank, the monkey leapt.

He sprang off the crocodile's back, grabbed the lowest branch, and swung himself up — up — up, as high as he could go, to the very top of the rose-apple tree. There he sat, panting, his heart (which was inside his chest all along, of course) thumping like a drum.

The crocodile waited at the bottom. "Well?" he called. "Have you got it? Hurry up, my wife is waiting!"

The monkey looked down at him. For a long time he didn't say anything. When he spoke, his voice was quiet and sad.

"You foolish creature. Did you really think anyone could take out their heart and hang it on a tree? My heart was with me all the time — and you nearly ate it."

The crocodile's mouth fell open. He understood, at last, that he had been tricked.

"Come down," he begged. "I was wrong. I'm sorry. We can still be friends —"

"No," said the monkey. "I gave you my fruit and my friendship and my trust, and you carried me into the middle of the river to give my heart to your wife. A friendship like that is like a broken pot. You can glue it back together, but it will never hold water again."

He picked one last rose-apple and dropped it, gently, onto the mud beside the crocodile.

"Go home," said the monkey. "Take this to your wife. It's the last fruit you'll get from my tree."

The crocodile picked up the rose-apple. He looked up at the monkey one last time. Then, slowly, he slid back into the river and swam away.

And he never came back.

Vishnu Sharma finished the story and looked at the three princes.

The eldest prince frowned. "But the monkey was so *small*. The crocodile could have eaten him in one bite."

"Yes," said the teacher.

"So how did he win?"

"Because," said Vishnu Sharma, "strength is not the only kind of power. The monkey couldn't fight, couldn't swim and couldn't run. But he could keep his head when everything around him was going wrong. Panic would have drowned him. Calm thinking carried him home."

The second prince said, "I think the crocodile was the real fool. He had a good friend, and he threw him away."

"That is another lesson," agreed the teacher. "Be careful who you listen to. The crocodile knew in his heart that what he was doing was wrong — and he did it anyway, because someone else demanded it."

The youngest prince, who had been very quiet, said: "I feel a little sorry for the crocodile."

Vishnu Sharma smiled. "So do I. That is the hardest lesson of all. Sometimes people who do wrong are not wicked — only weak. But even then, trust once broken is very hard to mend."

And so the three princes, who had once been the dullest boys in the kingdom, sat a little straighter, and thought a little harder, and waited for the next story.

**The moral:** *Presence of mind is a better friend than strength.*

summary: The Panchatantra is an ancient Sanskrit collection of animal fables, traditionally credited to Vishnu Sharma.
A monkey in a rose-apple tree befriends a crocodile by sharing fruit.
The crocodile's wife demands the monkey's 'sweet' heart.
The crocodile betrays his friend and carries him into the river.
In the middle of the river, the crocodile confesses his plan.
The monkey calmly claims he left his heart in the tree.
Back at the bank, the monkey escapes up the tree.
He ends the friendship: broken trust is like a cracked pot.
Main moral: presence of mind can save you when strength cannot.
Other lessons: think before you trust, don't betray friends under pressure.

rd-stories-moon-silver-slipper.title: Chanda Mama's Silver Slipper
rd-stories-moon-silver-slipper.subtitle: One night the Moon lost a slipper, and a little girl in Jaipur helped her find it.

sections.md:
Snuggle under your blanket. Is the window open a little? Can you see the sky?

Tonight's story is about **Chanda Mama**, the Moon, and a girl named **Meher** who lives on a rooftop house in Jaipur with her Dadi, a sleepy cat called Laddoo, and a pot of tulsi that smells like rain.

Grown-ups: read slowly. Pause at the questions in *italics* and let your little one answer. Each part takes about two minutes. If sleep comes early, simply stop — the Moon will wait for tomorrow.

sections.md:
After the story (maybe tomorrow morning!), you can chat about it together.

- Meher was **scared** of the dark rooftop at first. What helped her feel brave?
- Each friend she met gave her **one small help**. Can you remember them in order?
- Chanda Mama changes shape every night. That is not because she loses slippers! The Moon looks different because the Sun lights up a different part of her as she travels around the Earth.

**Did you know?** The Moon has no light of her own. She shines like a mirror, borrowing light from the Sun.

sections.md:
The story is make-believe, but the real Moon is full of wonders too. Here are some true things to whisper at bedtime:

- 🌍 **The Moon goes round the Earth.** One full trip takes about a month. That is why Dadi's calendar counts months by the Moon, and why many festivals come on special Moon days.
- 🌕 **Purnima and Amavasya.** The night the Moon is completely round is **Purnima** (full moon). The night we can't see her at all is **Amavasya** (new moon). **Diwali** comes on an Amavasya night — that's why we need so many lamps! **Guru Purnima** and **Sharad Purnima** come on full-moon nights.
- 🪞 **Borrowed light.** The Moon is a big ball of rock and dust. She shines only because sunlight bounces off her, like light from a mirror.
- 🐇 **Shadows on her face.** The grey patches are wide, flat plains. People in India sometimes see a rabbit in them; people elsewhere see a face.
- 🚀 **India went there!** India's spacecraft **Chandrayaan-3** landed gently near the Moon's south pole in August 2023, and a little rover named **Pragyan** rolled across the Moon's dust.
- 👣 **Footprints stay.** The Moon has no wind or rain, so footprints made there stay for a very, very long time.

check.q: What do we call the night when the Moon is completely round?
check.why: Purnima is the full-moon night, when the whole sunlit face of the Moon is turned towards us.

sections.h: A Moon diary (a game for two weeks)
sections.md:
Meher promised Chanda Mama she would look for her every night. You can make the same promise!

**You need:** a notebook, a pencil, and a grown-up to go out on the balcony or roof with you.

1. Start on a night when you see a thin, smiling crescent Moon in the evening sky, just after sunset.
2. Each night, at about the same time, look for the Moon. Draw her shape in a little circle in your notebook. Write the date (a grown-up can help).
3. If clouds hide her, draw a cloud and say, *Badal Bhed is giving someone a ride tonight!*
4. After about two weeks, look at your drawings. You will see the Moon grow from a thin curve to a half to a full round **Purnima** Moon — just as she promised Meher.

**Moon song to say together:**

> *Little bit, little bit, every night,*
> *Chanda Mama grows more bright.*
> *Slipper on, she walks the sky,*
> *Round and round, goodnight, goodbye!*

(Grown-ups: this little rhyme is written for this story — feel free to sing it to any tune.)

parts.md:
In the pink city of Jaipur, on top of a tall old house, there was a flat rooftop. On the rooftop there were three things: a pot of tulsi, a string bed called a charpai, and, every summer night, a little girl named **Meher**.

Meher slept on the roof with her Dadi when the nights were hot. Dadi told stories. Laddoo the cat curled up at their feet like a soft orange cushion. And above them, the whole sky stretched out like a big blue-black shawl sprinkled with sugar.

"Dadi," said Meher one night, "why is Chanda Mama so thin tonight? Yesterday she was round like a roti."

Dadi smiled her crinkly smile. "Perhaps she is walking somewhere far away, and we can only see a little of her face."

Meher looked and looked. Chanda Mama was a thin silver curve, like a smile without a face. And then — Meher sat up straight.

Something was falling from the sky.

It was small and shiny. It turned over and over, slowly, slowly, the way a leaf falls from a neem tree. It sparkled. It twinkled. And with a tiny sound — *tink!* — it landed right beside the tulsi pot.

*What do you think it was?*

Meher crept out of bed. The rooftop floor was still warm from the day's sun. She tiptoed to the tulsi pot and looked down.

There, lying on its side, was a **slipper**. A tiny silver slipper, no bigger than Meher's thumb. It glowed softly, like milk in moonlight. It had a curly toe, the kind that Rajasthani juttis have, and it was stitched all over with stars.

"Oh!" whispered Meher. She picked it up. It felt cool, like a drop of water.

Then she heard a voice. It was the softest voice she had ever heard, softer than Dadi's lullaby, softer than Laddoo's purr.

"Oh dear. Oh dear, oh dear. Where has it gone?"

Meher looked up. Chanda Mama was leaning down from the sky — just a little — and peering about with a worried face.

"Chanda Mama?" said Meher. "Are you looking for this?" She held up the silver slipper.

"My slipper!" said the Moon. "I was dancing across the sky and it slipped right off my foot. Without it I cannot walk all the way round to become full and round again. Little one, can you bring it back to me?"

Meher looked at the sky. It was very, very high.

"But how?" she asked. "I can't even reach the top shelf in our kitchen."

"Ask your friends of the night," said Chanda Mama. "Each one will help you a little bit. And a little bit, and a little bit, makes a lot."

Meher turned around. The rooftop looked different now. The water tank was a big dark lump. The corner by the stairs was full of shadows. Her tummy felt wobbly.

"I'm scared of the dark," she said in a small voice.

Just then, a tiny green-gold light blinked near the tulsi. On. Off. On.

"Hello," said the light. "I'm **Jugnu**. I'm a firefly. Are you the girl who is helping Chanda Mama?"

"Yes," said Meher. "But it's so dark."

"Dark is only the day taking a rest," said Jugnu. "Nothing in it has changed. The water tank is still the water tank. The stairs are still the stairs. Look — I'll show you."

Jugnu flew close to the water tank and blinked. It was just the old blue tank with Dadi's clothes-pegs on it. He flew to the corner. It was just the broom and a bucket.

Meher laughed. "It's only the broom!"

"You see?" said Jugnu. "Now, the first thing you need is a way to go higher. Follow my light. I know someone who lives at the top of the neem tree."

*Meher felt brave because she could see. What makes you feel brave at night?*

Meher held the silver slipper tight and followed the little blinking light across the roof, past the charpai where Dadi was gently snoring, to the place where the old neem tree spread its branches over the wall.

In the neem tree, on the very highest branch, sat a round grey owl with big yellow eyes. Her name was **Ullu Didi**.

"Hoo," said Ullu Didi. "Who is out so late?"

"It's me, Meher. I have to take Chanda Mama's slipper back to the sky."

Ullu Didi blinked one eye, then the other. "That is a long way. Even I cannot fly that high. But I can carry you to the top of the tallest place in Jaipur. From there, someone else can help."

"Will I be heavy?" asked Meher.

"Not if you think light thoughts," said Ullu Didi. "Think of feathers. Think of soap bubbles. Think of the steam from Dadi's chai."

So Meher closed her eyes and thought of feathers, and bubbles, and chai steam. And when she opened them — whoosh! — she was sitting on Ullu Didi's soft back, and they were flying!

Below them the city twinkled. Meher saw the old fort on the hill, lit up golden. She saw the long road with its little yellow street lamps like a necklace. She saw a train sliding past, its windows glowing like a row of diyas.

"It's beautiful," she whispered.

"The night is full of beautiful things," said Ullu Didi. "Most people are just asleep and miss them."

They flew up, up, to the top of the old fort's tallest tower, and Ullu Didi landed gently on the stone.

At the top of the tower, the wind was cool. Meher's hair blew across her face. Above her the sky was so close she felt she could almost touch the stars — but not quite.

"Now what?" she asked.

"Now," said Ullu Didi, "we wait for a friend who is always passing by."

They waited. Meher counted the stars. One, two, three... she got to twenty-seven and then lost count.

Then a soft white shape came drifting towards them. It was a **cloud** — a small, fluffy, rather shy cloud, shaped a little like a sheep.

"Good evening," said the cloud in a misty voice. "My name is **Badal Bhed**. I heard someone needs a ride upwards."

"That's me!" said Meher. "Can you really carry me?"

"Clouds are made of tiny, tiny drops of water," said Badal Bhed. "Too many drops and I'd be a rain cloud, and you'd get wet. But tonight I am just the right fluffiness for one small girl and one silver slipper."

Meher said thank you to Ullu Didi and gave her a gentle hug around her feathery neck. Then she stepped onto the cloud.

It was like stepping onto a mattress made of cotton candy. Her feet sank in a little. It was cool and slightly damp and smelled of the first rain on dry earth.

"Hold on," said Badal Bhed. "Up we go!"

Badal Bhed floated up and up. Jaipur grew smaller and smaller until it looked like a box of glittering bangles. But after a while, the cloud slowed down.

"Oh dear," said Badal Bhed. "I can only float as high as the air will hold me. I'm stuck."

Meher looked up. Chanda Mama was much closer now — big and bright and silver — but still too far to reach.

"Chanda Mama!" she called. "I'm here! But I can't get any higher!"

And then something rushed past them with a great *whooo-oosh*. It ruffled the cloud and made Meher's frock flap.

"Who's that?" she cried.

"That," laughed Badal Bhed, "is **Pavan**, the night wind. He's a bit of a show-off, but he has a kind heart."

Pavan came swirling back. "Did somebody need a push?" he whistled.

"Yes, please!" said Meher. "Just a little push. A gentle one."

"Gentle?" Pavan sounded surprised. "I'm usually busy blowing kites and rattling windows. But all right. I'll try gentle."

He took a big breath, and then — very softly, the way Dadi blows on hot milk — he blew.

Badal Bhed rose, and rose, and rose, until Meher was floating right beside the silver curve of the Moon.

Chanda Mama was enormous up close. Her face was pale and kind, with soft grey patches like the shadows on a sand dune. She smelled faintly of jasmine.

"You came," she said, smiling. "All the way from your rooftop!"

"I had help," said Meher. "Jugnu gave me light. Ullu Didi gave me wings. Badal Bhed gave me a ride. And Pavan gave me a push."

"A little bit, and a little bit, and a little bit," said Chanda Mama.

"Makes a lot!" said Meher.

She held out the tiny silver slipper. Chanda Mama stretched out one shining foot, and Meher slipped the slipper on. It fitted perfectly — *click*.

"Now I can finish my walk," said the Moon. "Every night I will step a little further, and every night you will see a little more of my face. In two weeks I'll be completely round. Will you look for me?"

"Every night," promised Meher.

Chanda Mama bent down and gave Meher a kiss on the forehead. It felt like a cool drop of dew. "Thank you, brave one. Now it is time for you to sleep."

*How do you think Meher felt now?*

Badal Bhed began to float down, down, slowly, like a feather. Pavan hummed a quiet tune. Below them Jaipur grew bigger — the bangles became streets, the streets became houses, and there was her own pink house with its flat roof and its tulsi pot.

On the neem tree, Ullu Didi hooted, "Goodnight!" Near the tulsi, Jugnu blinked his little lamp: on, off, on. *Goodnight.*

Meher stepped off the cloud onto the warm roof. She tiptoed past the water tank (just a water tank) and the corner (just a broom) and climbed back onto the charpai. Laddoo the cat opened one eye, yawned an enormous pink yawn, and went back to sleep.

Dadi stirred. "Meher? Were you awake, beta?"

"Only a little," said Meher. "Dadi, Chanda Mama is going to be round again soon."

"Is she?" murmured Dadi.

"Yes. She's got her slipper back now."

Dadi smiled in the dark and pulled the thin cotton sheet up to Meher's chin.

Meher looked up one last time. The thin silver Moon was a little brighter now, and just for a moment, Meher was sure she saw her wink.

Then Meher's eyes grew heavy, heavy, heavy, and she was fast asleep.

**And every night after that, Chanda Mama grew a little rounder — just as she had promised.**

*Goodnight, little one. Goodnight, Chanda Mama.*

sections.h: A word before we tune in
sections.md:
If you were young in India in the late 1960s, you may remember the weight of a valve radio warming up, the hiss before the station came in, the blue inland letter folded three ways, the week's wait for a reply. This story is for you — and for the grandchildren you might read it to.

It follows the **Srivastava family** of a rented house in Allahabad's Civil Lines over four summers, through the eyes of **Usha**, who is twelve when the story begins. The family and events are fictional; the world around them — the radio programmes, the prices, the long summers, the war winter of 1971 — is drawn from that time.

> Pour a cup of tea. This one is meant to be read slowly.

Readers who lived through these years often recall things like these. Tick the ones that bring back memories — and tell a grandchild the story behind one.

- The **inland letter** and the **postcard**, and the postman's bicycle bell.

- The **ration card** and queues for sugar or kerosene.
- **Surahi** water on summer afternoons, khus curtains sprinkled with water.
- Sleeping on the roof on charpais under the stars.
- **Film songs on the radio** on a weeknight, the whole mohalla listening together.

sections.md:
Writers of nostalgia aren't only describing the past — they are explaining what it *felt like*, which is what grandchildren most want to know. If this story stirs your own memories, try writing one small scene: a smell, a sound, a single afternoon. Don't worry about grammar. The details are the treasure.

*Did you know?* Many families kept their radio on a crocheted cover on top of the almirah, and a licence fee once had to be paid each year for owning a radio in India.

check.q: According to the note, what makes a memory scene come alive?
check.why: Small sensory details — a smell, a sound, an afternoon — make a memory vivid for the reader.

parts.md:
**May 1968.**

The radio arrived in a cardboard carton on the back of a cycle-rickshaw, with Babuji walking beside it the whole way from Katra market, one hand on the box as if it might jump off.

Usha was twelve. Her brother Pappu was eight. Their grandmother, Amma-ji, was seventy-something — nobody had ever written it down — and she sat on the takht in the veranda with her paan-box and watched the unpacking with the deep suspicion of someone who had seen the British leave and expected very little of new machines.

It was a Murphy, walnut-coloured, with a cloth front like a sari border and a long glass dial painted with the names of cities nobody in the family had seen: *Colombo*, *London*, *Moscow*, *Peking*. Babuji had paid for it in instalments. He had told nobody how much. Usha knew it was a great deal, because for a month afterwards there were no Sunday jalebis.

They put it on top of the almirah, on a white crocheted cover Mummy had made specially, and Babuji plugged it in and turned the big knob, and nothing happened.

“It has to warm up,” he said, a little desperately.

They waited. Pappu breathed on it. Then, from somewhere deep inside the walnut box, came an orange glow, and a hum, and a crackle like frying mustard seeds — and then a man's voice, clear as if he were sitting on the takht beside Amma-ji, reading the evening news.

Amma-ji put down her paan. “*Hai Ram*,” she said. “There's a man in the almirah.”

**Wednesday nights.**

Within a month, the whole household had organised itself around the radio, the way a house organises itself around a well.

Mornings were Babuji's: the news, the weather, the solemn voice reading the day's prices. Afternoons were Amma-ji's, who had discovered, to everyone's astonishment, that she adored the bhajans, and would sit with her eyes closed, nodding, correcting the singers under her breath.

But Wednesday nights belonged to everybody.

At eight o'clock, the film-song countdown came on from Ceylon, the signal swaying in and out like someone walking past a window. The neighbours' daughters, Kamla and Vimla, came over the wall. Mrs. D'Cruz from the next house sat in the doorway with her knitting. Even the dhobi's boy, who came for the clothes on Wednesdays, somehow timed his visit to the last fifteen minutes.

Usha kept a notebook, ruled into columns: *Song. Film. Singer. Position last week.* Kamla kept one too. They argued about the number-one spot as if their lives depended on it. When the signal faded at the crucial moment, there was an outcry, and Babuji would climb on a chair and turn the radio a quarter-inch to the left, and everyone would hold their breath.

Years later, in a different century, Usha would hear one of those songs in a supermarket in Pune and have to stand very still beside the rice shelves, because she was suddenly twelve years old in a room that smelled of mosquito coil and Amma-ji's paan, and Kamla was shouting *I told you it would go to number one!*

**Monsoon, 1968.**

Mummy's brother, Mama-ji, worked in the railways in faraway Bilaspur, and twice a month a blue inland letter arrived from him, folded three ways, its edges sealed with gum, the address written in his loopy hand.

The postman, Ram Prasad, rang his bicycle bell twice at the gate — two rings meant a letter, three meant a money order, one long ring meant a telegram, and a telegram meant trouble. Usha learned to tell from the kitchen, through the clatter of pans, how many rings there had been.

Mummy read the letters aloud in the evening, after the lamps were lit. They were mostly about nothing: the price of potatoes in Bilaspur, the neighbour's buffalo, a new colleague who sang too loudly. But Mama-ji always ended them the same way: *Write soon. A letter is half a meeting.*

Usha wrote back on Sundays. She had to fit everything into the blue paper, so she wrote smaller and smaller, until the last lines curled up the margins sideways. She told him about the radio, about the countdown, about Pappu falling into the neighbours' drain chasing a kite. It took a week to reach him. His reply took another. By the time she read his answer, she had forgotten what she'd asked.

It didn't matter. The waiting was part of it — the slow, hopeful waiting, like the ground waiting for rain.

**July 1969.**

The Americans were going to the Moon, and Babuji, who taught physics at the intermediate college, was more excited than Usha had ever seen him.

He explained it all at dinner with a steel tumbler for the Earth and a small lemon for the Moon, moving the lemon in great slow arcs while the dal went cold. *Three lakh eighty-four thousand kilometres*, he said, and Pappu said *how far is that in Allahabad-to-Bilaspur?* and Babuji worked it out on the back of the ration card and said *about four hundred and fifty times*, and Pappu was very impressed.

On the night of the landing — it was already the next morning in India — the whole street seemed to be awake. Babuji had the radio turned up as far as it would go. The news came through in pieces, broken up by static and the excited voices of announcers. Usha understood very little of the technical words. But she understood the moment when the announcer's voice changed, and Babuji grabbed Mummy's hand, and Amma-ji, who had been dozing, sat up and said, “What? What happened?”

“A man is standing on the Moon, Amma-ji,” said Babuji, and his voice shook.

Amma-ji looked out of the veranda at the Moon itself, pale over the neem tree. She looked for a long time.

“I can't see him,” she said finally. “But I'm glad somebody went. I used to think it was made of butter.”

**May 1970.**

The summer of 1970 was so hot that the tar on the Civil Lines road went soft and sucked at their chappals. The loo — that dry, scorching wind from the west — blew from eleven in the morning until five, and the whole city lay indoors behind khus curtains that Pappu was supposed to sprinkle with water every hour, and mostly forgot.

The family slept on the roof. Every evening at sunset, Usha and Pappu carried up the charpais and the cotton durries, and filled the earthen surahi from the hand-pump so the water would be cool by midnight. The stars were so thick over Allahabad then that Babuji could point out constellations with a torch: *Saptarishi*, the seven sages; *Dhruv tara*, the pole star that never moved.

And from the roof, faintly, they could hear radios all over the mohalla, a dozen of them tuned to the same station, a song drifting from roof to roof like a kite string, each house a fraction of a second behind the next, so the song had a soft echo the singer had never intended.

That was also the summer of the pressure cooker. Mummy had resisted for months — *my mother cooked dal for forty years without a whistle* — but when Mrs. D'Cruz brought one over and made rajma in twenty minutes, Mummy watched in silence, and the next week, a pressure cooker appeared in the Srivastava kitchen.

The first time it whistled, Amma-ji thought it was the radio announcing a war.

**December 1971.**

And then there was a war.

It came on the radio first, as everything did — the serious voices, the words *Pakistan* and *East Bengal* and *refugees*, which Usha had been hearing all year without quite understanding. Babuji listened to every bulletin now, standing, his face grave. He did not explain things with lemons and tumblers any more.

There were blackouts. At night, the city went dark on orders, and Mummy pasted brown paper over the window glass and they ate dinner by a single hurricane lantern turned low. The air-raid siren was tested once, and its long rising wail made Pappu, who was eleven now and said he was afraid of nothing, crawl into Usha's bed.

The radio was the only light that mattered. It sat on the almirah glowing its small orange glow and the whole family sat around it in the dark. Kamla's brother was in the army, posted somewhere in the east. When the news came through each evening, Kamla's mother would come over the wall and sit with Mummy, the two women holding hands without speaking.

The war lasted thirteen days. On the sixteenth of December, the radio announced that it was over — that a new country, Bangladesh, had been born. The streets filled with people. Somebody let off crackers left over from Diwali.

Kamla's brother came home in February, thin and quiet. He did not talk about it. He sat on the Srivastavas' veranda drinking tea, listening to the radio, and once Usha saw him close his eyes during a song, the way Amma-ji did during bhajans, and she understood that a song could be a kind of prayer.

**March 1972.**

Amma-ji fell ill at the end of winter. It was nothing sudden — she simply grew smaller, and slept more, and asked for the radio to be moved down from the almirah to the stool beside her bed.

One evening she said she wanted to speak to her son in Bilaspur.

There was no telephone in the house. Babuji went to the post office and booked a *trunk call* — the operator wrote it in a ledger, *Allahabad to Bilaspur, Lightning*, which cost extra and was supposed to be fast. Then they waited. Babuji sat on the post office bench for three hours with a newspaper he did not read. At last, a clerk shouted his name. He ran into the booth.

The line crackled and roared like the sea. Babuji shouted into it. From somewhere very far away, Mama-ji's voice shouted back. Neither could hear the other properly. *Amma — not well — come if you can*, Babuji shouted, and the line went dead.

Mama-ji came three days later, by the overnight train, carrying a basket of Bilaspur oranges. He sat by Amma-ji's bed and held her hand, and she opened her eyes and said, perfectly clearly, “You never write often enough.” And then she asked him to turn on the radio.

She died in April, on a Wednesday, as it happened, in the late afternoon, with the bhajans playing. Usha always thought she had chosen that day on purpose.

**July 1973.**

Usha left for college in Lucknow on a hot, wet morning, with a tin trunk, a bedroll, and a new notebook in which she had not yet written anything.

The radio was back on the almirah. It hummed a little louder now when it warmed up, and the dial light flickered, and Babuji said it needed a new valve and kept not buying one. Pappu, thirteen and suddenly taller than her, was using it every evening to listen to cricket commentary, leaning so close to the cloth speaker that he could have climbed inside.

At the station, Mummy pressed a parcel of puris and aloo into her hands and an inland letter, already addressed, already stamped. “Write soon,” she said. Then, as if she had only just remembered it: “A letter is half a meeting.”

On the train, Usha unfolded the blank inland letter on her knee and found that Babuji had written something in the corner in his small, careful physics-teacher hand:

*The Moon is three lakh eighty-four thousand kilometres away and a man walked on it. Lucknow is only two hundred. We will hear you clearly.*

She looked out of the window at the paddy fields going by, green and endless in the rain, and in her head — because she knew every word, because she had written it down in a column four summers before — she sang Wednesday night's number one, all the way to the end.

---

*Fifty years later, Usha has a phone that can play any song ever recorded. She still waits for Wednesday nights to listen to the old ones. Some habits are not habits. They are homes.*

summary: The Srivastava family of Allahabad buys a Murphy valve radio in May 1968.
The radio reorganises the household: news for Babuji, bhajans for Amma-ji, Wednesday night film-song countdowns for everyone.
Inland letters from Mama-ji in Bilaspur carry the refrain: 'A letter is half a meeting.'
In July 1969 the family listens to the Moon landing; Babuji explains it with a tumbler and a lemon.
Summer 1970: roof-sleeping, surahi water, the loo wind, and the arrival of the pressure cooker.
December 1971: war, blackouts, and the radio as the family's light; Bangladesh is born on 16 December.
1972: a trunk call booked for hours so Amma-ji can reach her son.
Amma-ji dies peacefully on a Wednesday, with bhajans playing.
1973: Usha leaves for college with a pre-stamped inland letter and her father's note.
Theme: the technologies of a time become the shape of family memory.
practice: Which detail in the story most reminded you of your own childhood? Write about it.

rd-stories-stepwell-cipher.title: The Stepwell Cipher
rd-stories-stepwell-cipher.subtitle: A dead grandfather's puzzle, a Jaipur stepwell, and a secret that is not treasure at all.

sections.md:
This mystery is a **puzzle-hunt**. You can solve the codes yourself before the characters do — the keys are all in the story.

**Zoya Qureshi**, thirteen, and her cousin **Arjun Mathur**, sixteen, spend the winter holidays in their late grandfather Nana's crumbling haveli in old Jaipur. Nana was a maths teacher who loved two things: stepwells and secret codes. In his desk they find a letter addressed to both of them, written in what looks like nonsense.

A third person wants that letter too.

sections.md:
Three codes appear in the story. Here is how each one works.

**1. Caesar shift.** Each letter moves a fixed number of places along the alphabet. With a shift of 3, A→D, B→E… To decode, move back 3. *KHOOR* → *HELLO*. Near the end of the alphabet you wrap around: X→A, Y→B, Z→C.

**2. Grid (Polybius) code.** Letters sit in a 5×5 grid (I and J share a box). Each letter becomes two numbers: row, then column. *2 3* = row 2, column 3 = H.

**3. Book code.** Numbers point to page–line–word in a book both people own.
