sections.h: Stepwells: engineering for a thirsty land
sections.md:
Nana's favourite places are real marvels. A **stepwell** (called *baori* or *bawdi* in Rajasthan and *vav* in Gujarat) is a deep well that you can walk down into, by flights of steps, to reach water far below the ground.

**Why build steps instead of using a rope and bucket?** In dry regions the **water table** — the level of water underground — rises after the monsoon and sinks lower and lower through the hot months. An ordinary well's rope might end up too short. A stepwell lets people simply walk further down as the water drops, all year round.

**Clever design features:**

- **Deep and narrow** at the bottom, so less water surface is exposed to the sun and less evaporates.
- **Stone walls** that stay cool; temperatures at the bottom can be noticeably lower than at the top on a summer afternoon.
- **Many steps on three sides** (as at Chand Baori) so lots of people can reach the water at once.
- **Pavilions, carvings and resting galleries**, because stepwells were also social places — for meeting, festivals and cooling off.

**Famous examples:** Chand Baori at Abhaneri near Jaipur (very old, with a famous criss-cross pattern of steps), Rani ki Vav at Patan in Gujarat (an 11th-century stepwell, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, carved with hundreds of sculptures), Adalaj Vav near Ahmedabad, and Agrasen ki Baoli in Delhi.

Many stepwells fell out of use when piped water and tubewells arrived and were filled with rubbish. Today some towns are cleaning and reviving them for **rainwater harvesting** — Nana would have approved.
keyTerms: Water table — the level below which the ground is full of water
Baori / vav — Rajasthani and Gujarati names for a stepwell
Heritage — places and traditions handed down that a community chooses to protect

check.why: As groundwater drops through the dry months, users simply go down more steps to reach it.

sections.md:
- **What counts as treasure?** The story asks whether money or memory is worth more.
- **Heritage.** Stepwells (*baoris* or *vavs*) were water-saving engineering and community spaces; many still survive in Rajasthan and Gujarat.
- **Trust inside families.** Arjun and Zoya begin as rivals and end as a team.
- **Facts over guesses.** Zoya refuses to blame the builder without evidence — and the intruder turns out to be someone else working for him.

*Did you know?* Chand Baori in Abhaneri, Rajasthan, has about 3,500 steps arranged over 13 storeys.

parts.md:
Nana's haveli smelled of old paper, marigolds and the paraffin he had used to oil his bicycle chain for fifty years. The bicycle still leaned against the courtyard pillar, as if he might come down the stairs any minute, adjust his spectacles and say, *Right. Who can tell me why a triangle is the strongest shape?*

He had died in October. Now it was December, and the family had come to Jaipur to decide what to do with the house.

“Sell it,” said Zoya's Mamu, on the phone in the courtyard, his voice carrying the way voices did off the old stone. “A builder has made a good offer. Very good.”

Zoya Qureshi, thirteen, sat on the study floor surrounded by Nana's notebooks. Her cousin Arjun Mathur, sixteen and too grown-up for most things, leaned in the doorway with his phone.

“It's just junk,” Arjun said.

“It's equations,” Zoya said. “And — look.” She held up an envelope she'd found taped under the desk drawer. On the front, in Nana's spiky handwriting: *For Zoya and Arjun. Together. Not separately.*

Inside was a single sheet. Every line was gibberish:

*JR WR WKH ZHOO. FRXQW WKH VWHSV.*

Arjun came and sat down. He did not say *junk* again.

“It's a cipher,” said Zoya. “He taught me this one when I was eight. Every letter moved along.”

“Moved how far?”

She chewed her pen. “He always said three was his lucky number. Three sides of a triangle.”

They wrote out the alphabet and slid each letter back three places. J became G. R became O. W became T. Slowly, letter by letter, the nonsense turned into words.

*GO TO THE WELL. COUNT THE STEPS.*

“The well,” said Arjun. “Which well? Jaipur's full of them.”

“Not *a* well. *The* well.” Zoya was already on her feet. “The stepwell behind Amer, the one near the fort. He took us there every winter. Don't you remember? He made us count the steps every single time and he always said we'd got it wrong.”

Arjun did remember, suddenly — the honey-coloured stone, the steps criss-crossing down in a pattern like a giant zip, Nana's voice echoing: *Again! Count again!*

That night, Zoya woke to a sound downstairs. A drawer sliding. By the time she reached the study with her phone torch, the room was empty, the window to the lane was open and Nana's notebooks were scattered across the floor.

The letter was safe. It was under her pillow.

In the morning, Mamu said it was a monkey. “They come in all the time in old Jaipur. Close the windows.”

“Monkeys don't open drawers in order,” said Zoya. “Left to right. Top to bottom.”

Arjun said nothing, but at breakfast he asked Mamu, casually, who the builder was.

“A Mr. Bhandari. Nice chap. He came to see the house twice when Nana was alive. Nana didn't like him much.” Mamu waved a paratha. “Your Nana didn't like anyone who wore shoes in the house.”

That afternoon they took an auto-rickshaw to the stepwell. It was a weekday, and quiet: a few tourists photographing the geometry, a man selling peanuts in paper cones, pigeons flicking across the green water at the bottom.

Zoya stood at the top step and felt, absurdly, like crying. Arjun bumped her shoulder lightly with his.

“Count,” he said. “Together. Not separately.”

They went down one flight, side by side, counting aloud. On the eleventh step from the top, carved into the vertical face of the stone where nobody would look unless they were crouching, were rows of small numbers, scratched neat as a maths exam:

*23 – 34 – 33 – 15 – 43 … 52 – 15 – 31 – 31*

“Nana,” said Arjun softly, “you vandal.”

They photographed the numbers and sat on the steps in the winter sun, working it out on the back of an auto-rickshaw receipt.

“Pairs,” said Zoya. “Always pairs. Never higher than five.”

“Grid,” said Arjun at once. “Five by five. Row and column. He did this with me once on a train to Delhi. I thought it was boring.” He drew the grid: A to E on the first row, F to K on the second, with I and J squeezed into one box.

*23* — row two, column three: H. *34* — row three, column four: O. *33* — N. *15* — E. *43* — S. *44* — T.

“Honest,” said Zoya. She kept going. The message took half an hour:

*HONEST WORK IS IN THE BOOK OF THE BEAUTIFUL. LOOK UNDER THE WELL.*

“Book of the beautiful,” said Arjun. “What's that supposed—”

“*Lilavati*,” Zoya breathed. “The old maths book. By Bhaskaracharya. *Lilavati* means something like *the beautiful one*. Nana had a translation, a really old one, with a red cloth cover. He used to read the puzzles to us at dinner.”

That was when Arjun said, very quietly, “Don't turn around. There's a man at the top of the steps in a white kurta who has been watching us since we arrived. And he is wearing shoes that cost more than my phone.”

They did not run, because running is the thing people notice. They walked up the far side of the stepwell, chatting loudly about lunch, bought a cone of peanuts from the seller, and got into the first auto they saw.

The man in the white kurta stood at the top of the steps and watched them go.

“Bhandari,” said Arjun. “Has to be.”

“We don't know that,” said Zoya. “Facts. Nana always said facts.” But her hands were shaking.

Back at the haveli, the red *Lilavati* was not on its shelf.

They searched for an hour. It was not in the study, the drawing room, or the trunk of old saris. Zoya sat down on the courtyard steps beside Nana's bicycle and put her face in her hands.

“He took it last night,” she said. “That's what he was looking for.”

Arjun was looking at the bicycle. At the battered leather saddlebag hanging from its seat, which nobody had touched in two months because touching it felt like touching Nana.

He unbuckled it. Inside, wrapped in a plastic bag against the dust, was a red cloth book.

“He never went anywhere without something to read,” Arjun said, and his voice cracked a little.

On the inside cover, in pencil, Nana had written a list of number triplets:

*47-3-2 · 112-8-5 · 9-1-4 · 201-12-7*

“Page, line, word,” said Zoya. “It's a book code. You can only solve it if you have the exact same edition.”

They turned the brittle pages. Page 47, line 3, word 2: *land*. Page 112, line 8, word 5: *given*. Page 9, line 1, word 4: *to*. Page 201, line 12, word 7: *school*.

*Land given to school.*

They stared at each other.

Pressed flat between pages 200 and 201 was a folded document on stamp paper, its creases soft with age. It was a registered gift deed, signed by Nana fifteen years before, giving the back half of the haveli's land — the overgrown garden with the old neem tree — to the small government school in the next lane, for a playground and a library. There was a covering letter from the school's headmistress thanking him, and a note in Nana's hand: *Copies with lawyer Sharma, Johari Bazaar. Tell the children when they are old enough to understand why.*

“So that's why the builder wants the letter,” said Arjun slowly. “If nobody knows about the deed, he buys the whole plot. Builds flats on the playground.”

“Look under the well,” Zoya read again. “*Under* the well.” She frowned. “But we found it in the book.”

“There's a well in the garden,” said Arjun. “A little one. Bricked over.”

The garden well was covered with a rusted iron plate. It took both of them, and a crowbar from the kitchen, to shift it. Underneath, a hand's depth below the rim, was a ledge — and on the ledge, a steel tiffin box sealed with wax.

Inside were two things. The first was a second copy of the deed, in case the first was lost. The second was a letter, written plainly this time, without any code.

*My dear Zoya and Arjun,*

*If you are reading this, you worked together, which is the only way I hid it. Arjun, you are good with systems; Zoya, you are good with memory. Neither alone is enough. That is also true of most things in life.*

*The school in the lane has been using the back garden for fifteen years. Children play cricket under the neem. Please do not let anybody take it away because they forgot, or because a builder offered a good price. A good price is not the same as a good thing.*

*I am sorry about the codes. I could not help myself.*

*Count the steps again next winter. You still have it wrong. It is 109 on the north side.*

*— Nana*

Zoya laughed and cried at the same time, which turned out to be possible.

Mamu read the letter twice in the courtyard. Then he went inside and made a phone call, and his voice was not loud this time.

The man in the white kurta came the next morning — not Bhandari, it turned out, but Bhandari's site manager, sent to 'have a look at the old papers' and, he admitted, to watch the children who seemed to be hunting for something. He had climbed in through the study window on the first night. When Mamu showed him the registered deed and the lawyer's name, he did not argue. He simply left, his expensive shoes clicking on the stone.

The haveli was not sold that year. The family decided to repair the front rooms and rent them to a small music school, and to put a proper fence around the playground with a gate onto the lane.

On the last day of the holidays, Zoya and Arjun walked to the government school. The headmistress, Mrs. Choudhary, was a small woman with chalk on her sleeves. When they told her about the codes, she laughed until she had to sit down.

“He came every Saturday,” she said. “To teach the older children maths puzzles. Always in a cipher. They called him *Code Sir*.”

Under the neem tree, a dozen children were playing cricket with a plank for a bat. Somebody hit a six over the wall.

Arjun watched the ball sail into the lane. “Next winter,” he said, “we count the steps again.”

“109,” said Zoya. “North side.”

“We'll see,” said Arjun, and for once he sounded exactly like Nana.

summary: Two cousins find a coded letter from their late grandfather, a maths teacher, in his Jaipur haveli.
Code 1 is a Caesar shift of 3: JR WR WKH ZHOO → GO TO THE WELL.
Code 2 is a 5×5 grid code carved on the 11th step of a stepwell.
'Book of the beautiful' points to Lilavati, the classic maths text by Bhaskaracharya.
Code 3 is a book code (page–line–word) that only works with the same edition.
The 'treasure' is a gift deed giving part of the land to a local school's playground.
A builder's man broke in to find the papers, hoping the gift would stay forgotten.
Nana designed the hunt so the cousins had to cooperate.
Theme: a good price is not the same as a good thing; memory and heritage matter.
Stepwells let people reach a falling water table; they were also community spaces.
Famous stepwells: Chand Baori (Abhaneri), Rani ki Vav (Patan, UNESCO), Adalaj, Agrasen ki Baoli.

rd-stories-stepwell-secret.title: The Secret of the Seventh Step
rd-stories-stepwell-secret.subtitle: Three cousins, a torn map, and a summer in Patan that turns into a treasure hunt through an ancient stepwell.

sections.md:
Summer holidays in **Patan**, an old town in north Gujarat, were supposed to be boring. No Wi-Fi at Motaba's house, no cousins your age except the two you already fight with, and a heat so thick you could slice it.

Then eleven-year-old **Kabir** found a piece of paper hidden inside the spine of an old book — and the summer cracked open.

This is an adventure story with **real puzzles**. Each time the cousins solve a clue, try to solve it yourself before you read on. The stepwell in the story is inspired by real stepwells (*vav*) of Gujarat, such as the famous Rani ki Vav in Patan, a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The family, the map and the treasure are made up.

**Kabir** (11) — loves books and old things, cautious, notices details.

**Zoya** (12) — Kabir's cousin, bold, fast, impatient; good at maths.

**Tinu** (8) — the youngest cousin, everyone underestimates him; he spots what the others miss.

**Motaba** — the cousins' great-grandmother, ninety-one years old and sharper than all of them.

**Themes to think about:** working as a team; patience versus speed; respecting heritage (the cousins never damage the stepwell); and the idea that the most valuable treasure is not always gold.

story.title: The Secret of the Seventh Step

parts.md:
The first rule of Motaba's house was: *don't touch the almirah*.

It was a tall wooden cupboard with brass handles, standing in the corner of the front room like a guard. Inside were books — hundreds of them — swollen and spotted with age, smelling of dust and neem leaves (Motaba put dried neem between the pages to keep insects away).

The second rule was: *don't go out in the afternoon heat*.

On the fourth day of the holidays, at two o'clock in the afternoon, when the whole of Patan was asleep and the ceiling fan was turning so slowly it seemed to be thinking about each rotation, Kabir broke the first rule.

He didn't mean anything by it. He was bored. His cousin Zoya was on the floor doing Sudoku puzzles in pen, "because pencil is for cowards". Little Tinu was lining up mango seeds on the windowsill in order of size. And Kabir had read every comic in the house twice.

So he opened the almirah.

The book he pulled out was bound in faded red cloth. The title was in Gujarati, which Kabir could read slowly: *Vav Ni Vaato* — Stories of the Stepwell. As he opened it, the spine cracked, and something slid out from inside the binding and floated to the floor.

It was a folded square of thick, yellowed paper.

Kabir unfolded it. His heart did a funny skip.

It was a drawing — in faded brown ink — of a stepwell, seen from the side, with its levels going down and down like a staircase into the earth. Seven levels. Next to the seventh, someone had drawn a small key. And under the drawing, in neat old-fashioned handwriting, were three lines:

*Count the queens who never sleep.*
*Find where shadow meets water at noon.*
*Ten lotuses — take away the ones that weep.*

The bottom corner of the paper was torn off.

"Zoya," said Kabir quietly. "Come and look at this."

Zoya looked. Then she looked again, and the Sudoku slid off her lap.

"It's a treasure map," she breathed.

"It's *probably* a doodle," said Kabir, though he didn't believe it either.

Tinu squeezed between them. "Why's there a key?"

That was the question. They spent the rest of the afternoon arguing about it in whispers. Zoya thought it was gold. Kabir thought it might be old documents. Tinu thought it was a dragon, and refused to be talked out of it.

At dinner — bajra rotlas, kadhi, and a heap of sweet mango ras — Kabir asked, as casually as he could, "Motaba, are there any stepwells near here?"

Motaba was ninety-one. She was tiny, wore white cotton saris, and had eyes like two bright black buttons. She put down her spoon.

"Near here? Beta, Patan is the city of stepwells. There's the big one, the Queen's one, that all the tourists visit. And there are small ones, forgotten ones, in the fields." She looked at Kabir for a long moment. "Why?"

"Just... a school project," said Kabir.

Zoya kicked him under the table. Motaba's eyes twinkled.

"There is one," Motaba said slowly, "behind the old Shiva temple at the edge of town. My grandfather used to take me there when I was smaller than Tinu. Seven levels deep. Nobody goes there any more." She picked up her spoon again. "It's not safe to go alone. If anybody wanted to go — for a school project — they would take Ramesh-bhai with them, and they would go early in the morning, before the heat."

Ramesh-bhai was Motaba's neighbour, a retired schoolteacher who walked everywhere with an umbrella, rain or shine.

"Yes, Motaba," said all three cousins at once.

They set off at six the next morning. The sky was pale gold, the air still cool, and the streets of Patan smelled of wet earth where people had sprinkled water in front of their doorways.

Ramesh-bhai led the way with his black umbrella, talking non-stop about the Solanki kings who ruled here nearly a thousand years ago. Zoya walked fast. Kabir walked carefully, the map folded inside his shirt pocket. Tinu ran ahead, came back, ran ahead again, like a puppy.

Behind the small Shiva temple, past a field of castor plants, they found it.

From above, it was just a long, narrow opening in the ground, edged with stone and half-hidden by a tangle of babool bushes. But when they pushed through and looked down, all three cousins went silent.

Steps. Steps going down and down, level after level, between walls carved with hundreds of figures — dancers, animals, flowers, gods and goddesses — all the soft gold colour of old sandstone. Pillars held up each level like the floors of an underground palace. And far, far below, at the very bottom, a dark green gleam: water.

"Whoa," whispered Tinu.

"Rules," said Ramesh-bhai, suddenly serious. "Walk, don't run. Stay on the steps, not the ledges. Touch nothing that might break. These carvings were made by hand, by people who have been dead for nine hundred years. They trusted us to look after them."

They went down slowly. With every level the air grew cooler, as if they were walking into a fridge. By the third level the sounds of the town had disappeared completely. There was only the echo of their footsteps and, somewhere, the drip of water.

Kabir pulled out the map.

"First clue," he said. "*Count the queens who never sleep.*"

"Queens," said Zoya. "So we need carvings of women with crowns."

There were dozens. Goddesses with many arms, dancers with jewelled belts, women holding mirrors, women holding lotuses, women with tiny babies.

"But which ones *never sleep*?" said Kabir.

They stared at the walls. Zoya started counting all the crowned figures and got to forty-three before giving up. "This is impossible."

Ramesh-bhai leaned on his umbrella and said nothing, but his moustache twitched as if he was trying not to smile.

Kabir sat down on a step and thought. *Never sleep.* Who never sleeps? Night-watchmen. Owls. Mothers of new babies. *The Sun?* No — the Sun sleeps every night...

Or does it? It just goes away. But it always *comes back*. From the east.

"Which way is east?" he said suddenly.

Ramesh-bhai pointed with his umbrella. "The opening runs east to west. That wall faces east — it's the one the morning sun lights first."

And it was true. On one side, early sunlight was already sliding down the carvings like warm honey. Those figures looked *awake*, eyes open, faces lit up. On the other side, the figures were still in deep shadow.

"The queens who never sleep are the ones who see the sunrise every day," said Kabir. "The ones facing east!"

They counted only the crowned queens on the sunlit east wall, top to bottom. Zoya counted. Kabir counted again to check.

"Seven," said Zoya.

"Seven," said Kabir.

"Seven levels," said Tinu. "Seventh step." He pointed at the key drawn on the map. "It's telling us to go to the seventh level. The bottom!"

Zoya high-fived him so hard he nearly fell over.

The seventh level was right at the bottom, a stone platform at the edge of the water. The water was deep and green and perfectly still, reflecting the patch of sky far above like a round blue eye.

"Second clue," said Kabir. "*Find where shadow meets water at noon.*"

It was only seven-thirty.

"We can't wait four and a half hours down here," said Zoya. "Motaba will send the police."

"We don't have to wait," said Kabir slowly. "We can *work it out*."

He remembered something from his science class. At noon, the Sun is at its highest point in the sky. Shadows are at their shortest. Here in Gujarat in summer, the noon Sun is almost directly overhead — so the light would fall nearly straight down the narrow shaft of the stepwell.

"At noon," he said, "the sunlight comes straight down through the opening. So the edge of the shadow — where the bright part stops — would be right under the edge of the opening at the top."

Zoya was already looking up, squinting. "The top opening isn't straight. Look — on the west side there's that stone beam sticking out. That's what would make the shadow."

They lined it up as best they could, Kabir standing on the platform, Zoya calling "left — no, your other left — stop!" from the step above, using the stone beam high overhead as her guide.

Kabir ended up standing at the very edge of the platform, at a spot where the stone met the water. In the wall just there, at knee height, was a carved panel. And in that panel was a row of lotus flowers.

Tinu crouched down beside him. "Ten," he said, counting with his finger in the air, not touching. "Ten lotuses. That's the third clue!"

*Ten lotuses — take away the ones that weep.*

The ten lotuses were carved in a neat row, each one about the size of Kabir's palm, each with layers of petals opening outwards.

"Weeping lotuses?" said Zoya. "Lotuses don't cry."

They stared and stared. Kabir thought maybe some were drooping. Zoya thought maybe some were facing down. Neither idea worked.

It was Tinu, crouched lowest, nose almost on the stone, who said: "Some of them are wet."

They bent down. He was right. Most of the carving was dry, but three of the lotuses — the second, the fifth and the ninth — had a thin dark trickle of water seeping out from a crack at their centre and running down the stone. Like tears.

"Weeping!" said Zoya. "Tinu, you genius!"

Tinu went pink.

"Ten take away three," said Zoya, instantly. "Seven. Again! Seven queens, seventh step, seven lotuses."

"So we want the seven that aren't weeping," said Kabir. "But what do we do with them?"

He looked at the map again. The torn corner. There must have been something there, once — instructions. Now there was only the key.

Ramesh-bhai cleared his throat. "May I?" He bent and looked carefully, without touching. "Interesting. The dry lotuses each have a small hollow at the centre. The weeping ones have a crack — perhaps water got in over the centuries and broke them."

"Like little keyholes," said Kabir. "But we don't have a key."

Zoya groaned. "Of course we don't. The key's in the *picture*."

And then Kabir remembered something. Something he'd felt when he opened the old red book, but ignored: a hard little bump inside the back cover.

They raced back up all seven levels (*walk, don't run!* Ramesh-bhai called after them, puffing), through the castor field, down the lanes of Patan, and burst into Motaba's front room so fast that a pigeon flew off the windowsill.

Motaba was sitting in her chair with a cup of tea. On her lap was the old red book.

"Looking for this?" she said.

The cousins froze.

Motaba opened the back cover. Under the cloth was a slit, and from it she slid out a thin piece of metal: a small, flat brass key, green with age, with a lotus shape at its end.

"You knew," said Kabir.

"I put the map in that book myself," said Motaba, "seventy-nine years ago. When I was twelve. My grandfather made the puzzle for me, the summer before he died. I solved the first two clues, but I was too scared to go down to the seventh step alone, and then the family moved away to Ahmedabad." She turned the key over in her small wrinkled fingers. "I always wondered if one of my grandchildren would find it. I didn't expect it would take three of my great-grandchildren."

Zoya, for once, had nothing to say.

"Well?" said Motaba, putting down her tea and reaching for her walking stick. "It's only nine o'clock. Before the heat. Ramesh-bhai, would you mind going back once more? And Tinu, beta, you'll have to hold my hand on the steps."

Tinu took her hand very seriously, as if it were made of glass.

It took a long time to get Motaba down seven levels. She went one step at a time, Tinu on one side, Ramesh-bhai on the other. Every few levels she stopped and looked at the carvings, and said things like, "*That* elephant — I remember him! He has a chipped ear."

At last they reached the platform by the water. Motaba lowered herself onto the step and looked at the row of lotuses for a long time.

"Seven dry ones," said Kabir. "But which one does the key go in?"

Motaba smiled. "My grandfather loved the number seven. Count to the seventh *dry* lotus."

They counted, skipping the three weeping ones: one, three, four, six, seven, eight — and *ten*. The last lotus.

Zoya looked at Kabir. Kabir looked at Motaba. Motaba held out the key to Tinu.

"You found the weeping ones," she said. "You do it."

Tinu's hand was shaking. He fitted the little brass key into the hollow at the centre of the tenth lotus. It slid in with a gritty *scrape*. He turned it.

*Click.*

The small square stone just below the lotus panel shifted outward by a finger's width. Kabir and Zoya, very gently, eased it out. Behind it was a little hollow in the wall, dry as dust. And inside the hollow was a tin box, the kind people once kept biscuits in, wrapped in oilcloth.

No gold. No dragon.

Inside the tin were a bundle of letters, tied with string; a black-and-white photograph of a stern old man with a white moustache, holding a small girl on his knee; and a notebook, its pages full of drawings of every carving in the stepwell, each one labelled in that neat old-fashioned handwriting.

Motaba held the photograph for a long, long time. Nobody said anything. Water dripped somewhere in the dark. The circle of sky above them had turned bright, hot blue.

"That's me," she said at last, touching the little girl. "And that's him. Bapuji."

She opened the notebook. On the first page was written: *For my Kusum, who notices things. So that someone remembers what is carved here, even when the well is forgotten.*

"He drew all of them?" whispered Kabir, turning the pages. Elephants. Dancers. Queens. Lotuses — even the weeping ones, drawn before they cracked.

"Every single one," said Motaba. "He was a stonemason's son. He said a stepwell is a library made of stone, and every carving is a story." She looked at the three of them. "He would have liked you."

That evening, the cousins didn't fight once. They sat on the floor of the front room around the tin box while Motaba read the old letters aloud, and told stories they had never heard — about her grandfather, about Patan long ago, about the summer she was twelve.

Zoya started a list of all the carvings in Bapuji's notebook, checking each one against the real wall. ("Next time," she said, "we count *properly*. In pen.") Kabir began writing it all down — this story, in fact. And Tinu fell asleep with the brass lotus key clutched in his hand.

At the end of the holidays, Motaba gave the notebook to the local heritage society, so that the forgotten stepwell could be studied and protected. The newspaper in Patan printed a photo: one very old lady and three cousins, standing at the top of seven levels of golden stone.

The headline said: *Lost Notebook Saves Lost Well.*

Tinu said it should have said *Dragon Not Found*. But he was smiling when he said it.

summary: Kabir finds a hidden map of a seven-level stepwell in an old book at Motaba's house in Patan.
Three clues: queens who never sleep, shadow meets water at noon, ten lotuses minus the weeping ones.
The 'queens who never sleep' are the seven crowned figures on the sunlit east wall.
The noon-shadow clue is solved using the science of a high midday Sun.
Tinu notices three wet, cracked lotuses: 10 − 3 = 7.
Motaba reveals she hid the map at age twelve; her grandfather made the puzzle.
The key opens a hollow behind the tenth lotus.
The treasure is letters, a photo and a notebook of drawings of every carving.
The notebook goes to a heritage society to protect the stepwell.
Themes: teamwork, observation, respecting heritage, family memory.

rd-stories-sundarbans-tide.subtitle: A storm, a drifting boat and two children lost among the mangroves of the Sundarbans — with only their wits and their grandmother's lessons.

sections.md:
The **Sundarbans** is the largest mangrove forest in the world, spread across the delta where the Ganga, Brahmaputra and Meghna rivers meet the Bay of Bengal, shared by India and Bangladesh. It is a maze of islands and channels where the sea comes in and goes out twice every day. Trees stand on roots like stilts. Crabs click in the mud. And somewhere, quiet and unseen, the Royal Bengal tiger walks.

This story follows **Mitali** (12) and her brother **Bablu** (9), who live on Gosaba island at the forest's edge. One afternoon, a sudden storm snaps their boat's rope — and the tide carries them deep into the forest.

The children and their village are fictional, but the forest facts are real.

sections.h: The forest science in the story
sections.md:
Mitali survives by remembering what her grandmother, Thakuma, taught her. Every one of these is true of the Sundarbans:

- **Two high tides and two low tides a day.** The Moon's pull makes the sea rise and fall roughly every six hours. At low tide, channels become mud; at high tide, the same mud is under water.
- **Mangroves breathe through their roots.** Mangrove mud has very little oxygen, so many mangroves grow pencil-like roots called *pneumatophores* that poke up out of the mud to take in air.
- **Water in the channels is salty or brackish** — not safe to drink. Rainwater is fresh.
- **Tigers here swim well** and the forest is their home. People who work in the forest travel in groups, stay in boats when possible and respect the forest's rules.
- **Going out with the tide, coming back with the tide.** Boatmen use the flow of the tide like a free engine.

**Did you know?** The mangroves of the Sundarbans protect millions of people by softening the force of cyclones and storm waves before they reach villages.

check.why: Sundarbans channels mix sea water with river water, so it is salty; the children collected rainwater instead, which is fresh.

sections.md:
Mitali is scared almost the whole time — and still makes good decisions. Courage in this story is not about having no fear; it is about thinking clearly *with* fear.

The forest is not the villain either. The storm, the tide and the tiger are all simply part of the place. The children survive because they understand it and respect it.

**Themes:** knowledge passed between generations; staying calm; protecting younger siblings; respect for nature; how communities search together.

check.q: What did Thakuma mean by 'the river always comes back'?
options: The tide returns every few hours, so waiting can be the best plan
check.why: Because tides rise and fall on a regular cycle, a boat stuck on mud will float again when the water returns — so patience is a strategy.

parts.md:
On Gosaba island, everyone could read the river.

Mitali had learned before she could read books. She knew that when the water in front of their house slid away from the steps and the mud gleamed like wet chocolate, the tide was going out — *bhata*. She knew that when it came creeping back, filling the crab holes and lifting the boats, it was coming in — *jowar*. She knew that it happened twice every day, but never at exactly the same time, because it followed the Moon, not the clock.

Her grandmother, Thakuma, had taught her. Thakuma had been a honey collector's wife, and later a teacher in the island school, and she knew the forest across the river better than anyone.

"The forest has rules," Thakuma always said, tapping Mitali's forehead. "Learn them, and the forest lets you live beside it. Forget them, and it doesn't care how clever you are."

There were many rules. Never go into the forest alone. Never stand at the edge of the water at dusk. Always know which way the tide is going. Never drink the river water, however thirsty you are. And if you meet Dakshin Rai's cat — that was what the old people called the tiger — be still, be big, and never, ever turn your back and run.

Mitali was twelve. Her brother Bablu was nine and thought rules were mostly for other people.

That afternoon in late September, their father had gone to the market at Canning with the big boat. Their mother was at the self-help group meeting. Thakuma was asleep after lunch. And Bablu wanted to look at the crabs.

"Just to the end of the jetty," Bablu begged. "In the small boat. It's *tied up*, Didi. We won't even move."

The small boat was a wooden dinghy, hardly bigger than a bed, tied to a bamboo post at the end of the family's little jetty. Their father used it to check the fish nets close to shore.

Mitali looked at the sky. It was hot and white, the kind of sky that made your head ache. Far to the south, over the sea, there was a smudge of dark grey.

"Ten minutes," she said. "And then we come in."

They climbed in. The boat rocked gently. Bablu leaned over the side, watching the red-clawed fiddler crabs waving their one big claw on the mud bank, as if they were all conducting an orchestra.

The smudge of grey grew. Mitali didn't notice. Bablu was telling her a long story about a crab that had stolen his shoe.

Then the wind came.

It came all at once, with a roar like a train, flattening the water and bending the palm trees in the village. Rain followed, so hard and thick it felt like being hit with handfuls of gravel. The little boat bucked. The bamboo post creaked. Mitali grabbed for the rope —

*SNAP.*

The old rope broke. And the tide, which was going out, took them.

They shot away from the jetty, spinning slowly, into the wide brown river. Mitali screamed for Thakuma, but the wind tore the sound away. Within a minute, Gosaba was a grey shape behind the rain. Within five, it was gone.

There were no oars. Bablu had taken them out to make room for his legs.

Mitali held on to the sides of the boat and made herself think. *Which way is the tide going?* Out. Towards the sea. Into the forest.

The boat swept across the big river and into a narrower channel, and suddenly the forest was all around them. Mangrove trees leaned in from both banks, their roots arching into the water like the legs of enormous spiders. Rain dripped from every leaf. The light turned green and dim.

Bablu had stopped talking. His face was white. "Didi," he whispered. "Are we in the *jungle*?"

"Yes."

"Is there — are there —"

"Yes," said Mitali. There was no point lying. Bablu knew. Everyone on Gosaba knew. "But tigers don't want to meet us any more than we want to meet them. We're going to be quiet and sensible and stay in the boat. Thakuma says the boat is the safest place."

The channel twisted and split, and split again. Every turn looked the same: brown water, grey rain, green leaves, black roots. Mitali tried to remember the turns — left, right, right — but soon she lost count.

After about an hour, the storm passed as quickly as it had come. The rain thinned to a drizzle, then stopped. Water dripped everywhere. Somewhere a kingfisher called — a sharp, bright *ki-ki-ki*.

And the boat slowed down. Because the water was going away.

By six o'clock, the boat was sitting on mud.

The channel that had been wide enough to float a bus was now a shallow, sticky gully. All around, the mud was full of strange things sticking up — hundreds and thousands of thin, pointed roots, like pencils pushed into the ground, like a bed of nails.

"What *are* those?" said Bablu.

"Breathing roots," said Mitali. She remembered Thakuma pulling one gently and showing her. "The mud has no air in it, so the trees grow roots that stick up like snorkels. They breathe through them."

"Trees with snorkels," said Bablu, and for a second, he almost smiled.

They were stuck. There was no way to push the boat through the mud, and Mitali knew — it was one of Thakuma's strictest rules — that you never, ever climbed out onto the mud of the forest. You could sink to your knees. And you didn't know who might be watching from the trees.

So they sat. The sun set. Mosquitoes came out in whining clouds. Bablu was thirsty and wanted to scoop up some of the water still lying in the gully.

"No," said Mitali, grabbing his wrist. "It's salty. It'll make you sicker."

Then she had an idea. The bottom of the boat was full of rainwater from the storm — but it was mixed with mud from Bablu's feet. Mitali took off her dupatta and folded it four times. She held it over the steel tiffin box that Bablu had brought (of course Bablu had brought snacks), and slowly squeezed rainwater from the boat's seat-cloth through the dupatta into the tiffin.

It was a bit brown. It tasted of cloth. But it was fresh. They each drank half.

"Thakuma says," said Mitali, as the darkness came down like a lid, "that the river always comes back. We just have to wait."

Night in the forest was louder than day.

Frogs boomed. Insects shrilled. Something splashed in the distance — a fish? an otter? Mud popped and bubbled as crabs moved through it. Leaves rustled. Every rustle made Mitali's heart jump.

Bablu curled up in the bottom of the boat with his head in her lap. "Tell me a story, Didi."

So she told him one of Thakuma's: the story of Bonbibi, the lady of the forest, who protects the poor and the honest people who enter the forest only for what they need. Mitali's voice shook at first, but as the story went on, it steadied.

At about nine o'clock — Mitali guessed it from the stars that had come out between the clouds — she felt the boat shift.

It was the smallest thing. A little wobble. Then a gentle lift.

"Bablu," she whispered. "Feel that?"

The water was coming back. It slid silently in from the darkness, covering the breathing roots one by one, filling the crab holes, lifting the boat off the mud. Within an hour, they were floating again. And still it rose, higher and higher, until the water was among the lower branches of the mangroves.

"Which way do we go?" asked Bablu.

Mitali thought hard. The tide was coming *in*, so it was flowing *away* from the sea, deeper into the forest — and maybe away from home, too. If they drifted with it now, they might get even more lost.

"We don't go anywhere yet," she said. She looped her dupatta around a low branch and tied the boat to it. "We wait for the tide to turn. The tide that brought us in will take us out."

Some time after midnight, the frogs stopped.

All of them, at once. The insects fell silent too. The whole forest went still, as if it was holding its breath.

Mitali felt the hairs on her arms stand up. She didn't know how she knew, but she knew.

Slowly, very slowly, she turned her head.

On the bank, not twenty metres away, half-hidden by roots and shadow, were two eyes. They caught the faint moonlight and glowed a pale greenish-gold. They didn't blink.

Bablu was asleep. Mitali put a hand on his shoulder and kept it there, very gently, so he wouldn't wake and cry out.

*Be still. Be big. Never turn your back.*

She sat up as straight and tall as she could. She did not look away. She did not move. Her heart was thundering so loudly she was sure the tiger could hear it.

The eyes watched her. The forest held its breath.

She didn't know how long it lasted. A minute. An hour. Then, as silently as it had come, the shape on the bank turned — she caught a glimpse of a long striped body, a heavy shoulder, the swing of a tail — and melted away into the dark mangroves without a sound.

One frog croaked. Then another. Then the whole forest started up again, as if nothing had happened.

Mitali let out a breath she felt she had been holding all her life. Her hands were shaking so badly she had to sit on them.

Bablu stirred and mumbled, "Didi? What is it?"

"Nothing," she said. Her voice came out strange. "Go back to sleep. The forest is just saying goodnight."

Mitali didn't sleep. She watched the water.

Just before dawn, when the sky in the east was turning from black to dark blue, she saw a leaf floating past the boat. It was floating the *other way*.

The tide had turned.

"Bablu! Wake up! We're going home."

She untied her dupatta. The boat swung round and began to drift, slowly at first, then faster, as the water poured out of the forest towards the sea, carrying them with it.

But channels split. At every fork, she had to choose. Mitali leaned over the side and watched which way the most leaves and twigs were moving, and which way the current pulled hardest. *Follow the biggest water*, Thakuma had once said. *Small channels go into the forest. Big channels go to the river.*

So at every fork, Mitali pushed off a root with her hands to steer them into the wider, faster stream. Bablu helped, paddling with the lid of the tiffin box. Their arms ached. Their fingers were cut by the sharp oyster shells clinging to the roots. But the channels grew wider, and wider.

And then, as the sun rose orange and enormous through the mist, the trees fell away on either side, and they shot out into a huge, open river so wide they could barely see the far bank.

And on that river, in the morning light, was a boat. Then another. Then five, ten, twenty boats, spread out in a long line across the water, and on every one of them people were shouting and waving.

The whole of Gosaba had come to look for them.

Their father reached them first. He jumped from his boat into theirs so hard he nearly sank it, and held them both so tightly Bablu squeaked. He was crying and laughing at the same time and didn't seem to notice.

The boats had been searching all night, with torches and lanterns and the Forest Department's motor launch. But the forest was huge, and the channels were a maze, and at high tide everything looked different. They had nearly given up hope.

"How did you get *out*?" asked one of the forest guards — a young woman in a khaki uniform who had been searching since the storm. "You came out of a channel we'd already checked twice."

"We waited for the tide to turn," said Mitali. "And then we followed the biggest water."

The guard looked at her for a long moment. "Who taught you that?"

Back on Gosaba, Thakuma was waiting at the end of the jetty, where the snapped rope still hung from the bamboo post. She was very small and very old, and she had been standing there all night. She didn't say anything at first. She just held Mitali's face in her two wrinkled hands and looked at her.

Later, after hot rice and dal and a very long sleep, Mitali told her about the eyes on the bank.

Thakuma nodded slowly. "You were still?"

"Yes."

"You didn't run?"

"No."

"Then you remembered the rules," said Thakuma. "And the forest let you go home."

That winter, the forest guard came to Gosaba school to talk about the Sundarbans. She asked Mitali to stand up and tell the class what she had done. And at the end she said: "When you're older, if you want to, come and train with us. We need people who can read the river."

Mitali thought about it every day after that. And Bablu? Bablu never touched the small boat again without checking the rope twice.

summary: Mitali (12) and Bablu (9) live on Gosaba island in the Sundarbans.
Thakuma has taught Mitali the forest's rules and how tides work.
A sudden storm snaps the boat's rope; the ebb tide carries them into the forest.
At low tide they are stranded on mud among breathing roots (pneumatophores).
Mitali filters rainwater through her dupatta because river water is salty.
She ties the boat during the rising tide instead of drifting deeper in.
A tiger watches them at night; Mitali stays still and tall, and it leaves.
At dawn she rides the falling tide out, always choosing the bigger channel.
The whole village is searching; they are found on the main river.
Themes: calm thinking, inherited knowledge, respect for nature and community.

sections.md:
The **Vetala Panchavimshati** — 'Twenty-five Tales of the Vetala' — is a very old Sanskrit collection. A famous version appears in the 11th-century *Kathasaritsagara* ('Ocean of the Streams of Stories') compiled by **Somadeva** in Kashmir. Over centuries it was retold in Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and many more languages, and generations of Indian children met it through comics and a much-loved television serial.

The **frame story**: a brave king, usually called **Vikramaditya** (or Trivikramasena in Somadeva), promises a mysterious ascetic that he will fetch a corpse hanging from a tree in a cremation ground. The corpse is possessed by a **vetala** (Betaal), a clever spirit. As Vikram carries it, the Betaal tells a story ending in a riddle. The rule: *if the king knows the answer and stays silent, his head will burst; if he speaks, the Betaal flies back to the tree.* Being wise and honest, Vikram always answers — and has to start again.

This is a retelling in our own words.

sections.md:
**Vikramaditya** — 'the sun of valour' — is the legendary king of **Ujjain** (in today's Madhya Pradesh), famous in Indian folklore for courage, generosity and justice. Many story cycles gather around him: the Betaal tales, the *Simhasana Dvatrimshika* (the thirty-two statues of his throne, each telling a story of his virtue), and legends of his court of nine learned 'jewels'.

Historians are careful here. Several real kings used the title *Vikramaditya* — the Gupta emperor **Chandragupta II** (who ruled around 375–415 CE) is the best-known example — and the popular **Vikram Samvat** calendar, which begins in 57 BCE, is traditionally linked to a King Vikramaditya. But scholars disagree about whether the legendary Vikram of Ujjain was one specific person, a memory of several rulers blended together, or mostly a figure of story. In this read, he is the hero of a folk tradition, not a figure from a history textbook.

What matters for the tales is his character: a king strong enough to walk alone through a cremation ground at midnight, and wise enough to judge the hardest questions fairly.
keyTerms: Vikram Samvat — a calendar era starting in 57 BCE, still used in parts of India and in Nepal
Ujjain — ancient city on the Shipra river, legendary capital of Vikramaditya
Legend — a traditional story that may be loosely linked to real people or places

sections.md:
The tale asks a question philosophers still argue about: **what makes a person who they are?** Is it the body, the face, the memories, the mind?

Vikram's traditional answer is that the one with the **husband's head** is the husband, because the head is the 'chief' of the body and carries the mind. Some retellings argue it differently, and Thomas Mann wrote a whole German novella, *The Transposed Heads* (1940), inspired by this Indian tale.

You may disagree with the king. That is the point of the game.

sections.h: Debate corner: how to answer a Betaal riddle
sections.md:
The Betaal does not want *any* answer — he wants a **reasoned** one. You can practise the same skill in class or at the dinner table.

**Step 1 — State your answer clearly.** *'The husband is the one with Dhavala's head.'*

**Step 2 — Give your main reason.** *'The head holds the mind and memory, and these make us who we are.'*

**Step 3 — Support it with evidence from the story.** *'The man with Dhavala's head remembers the wedding; the other man remembers being her brother.'*

**Step 4 — Face the strongest objection.** *'Someone might say the body took the marriage vows. But a body without the memory of a promise cannot keep it.'*

**Step 5 — Conclude.** Restate your answer, perhaps with a fairer suggestion: *'She should also respect what both men feel, and the brother deserves care as he adjusts.'*

This five-step pattern — **claim, reason, evidence, counter-argument, conclusion** — works for exam answers, debates and essays alike. Try it for the opposite side too: a good thinker can argue both and then decide.

> Did you know? Modern discussions about organ transplants, memory loss and even artificial intelligence keep returning to the Betaal's question: is a person their body, their memories, or something more?

check.q: In a reasoned answer, what is the 'counter-argument' step for?
options: Facing the strongest objection to your view and answering it
check.why: Addressing the best opposing point shows your answer has been tested, which makes it more convincing.

sections.md:
- **Haste has consequences.** Madanasundari's panic causes the confusion; good intentions are not enough without care.
- **Rash vows.** Dhavala's secret, unclear promise leads to tragedy; the goddess herself calls it badly judged. The story does not praise self-harm — it warns against it.
- **Identity.** A question as fresh today — in debates about memory, AI and transplants — as a thousand years ago.
- **Story within a story.** The *frame narrative* appears across Indian literature: the Panchatantra, the *Mahabharata*, and later the Arabian Nights.
- **Language:** *vetala* (a spirit that can inhabit corpses), *ascetic* (a person who gives up comforts for spiritual practice), *ghat* (steps down to a river), *dark fortnight* (the waning half of the lunar month).

*Did you know?* 'Vetala' spirits in Sanskrit lore were not simply evil; they were often tricksters who tested people with knowledge.

story.title: The Tale of the Exchanged Heads

parts.md:
The night was so dark that the river below the cremation ground could only be heard, not seen. King Vikram walked between the dying fires, his sword drawn, his bare feet sure on the ash.

He had made a promise. A thin, smiling ascetic had come to his court every day for twelve years, each time presenting a single fruit, and each fruit, when cut open, held a ruby. When at last the king asked what he wanted in return, the ascetic said: *On the fourteenth night of the dark fortnight, come alone to the great burning-ground. On the old peepal tree hangs a body. Bring it to me, and say nothing on the way.*

Kings who accept rubies must keep promises.

The tree was enormous, its roots knotted like old rope. From one branch hung a corpse, pale and swaying slightly though there was no wind. Vikram climbed, cut the rope, and the body fell — and laughed.

It was not the laugh of a dead man. It was high and amused and very much awake.

Vikram climbed down, hoisted the body over his shoulder, and began to walk. The body was cold and strangely light, and it smelled of rain.

“A long road, King,” said a voice by his ear. “Shall I tell you a story to pass the time?”

Vikram said nothing.

“I'll take that as a yes,” said the Betaal.

“But first, the rules,” the Betaal went on cheerfully. “At the end of my story I shall ask you a question. If you know the answer and keep quiet, your head will burst into a hundred pieces. If you answer — well. You spoke, didn't you? And the promise was silence. So I shall fly back to my tree.” It sighed contentedly. “I do enjoy this.”

Vikram walked on. The fires behind them sank to embers.

“Once,” began the Betaal, “in a town by a river, there lived a washerman's son named Dhavala. One day, at a festival, he saw a young woman bathing at the ghat with her friends — Madanasundari, her name was, *beautiful as the god of love* — and he fell so completely in love that he could not eat for a week.”

“His friends teased him. His mother worried. Finally his father, a practical man, went to Madanasundari's family, and since they were of the same community and the young people liked each other, the wedding was arranged.

“Now, Dhavala was a devotee of the goddess, whose temple stood alone on a hill outside the town. In his longing, he had made a vow in his heart: *If I marry Madanasundari, I will offer the goddess the greatest gift I have.* He did not say what that gift was. He had not, perhaps, thought very carefully.”

“Some months after the wedding,” the Betaal went on, “Dhavala, Madanasundari and her brother set out together to visit her parents in a nearby village. On the way they passed the hill with the goddess's temple.

“Dhavala stopped. He remembered his vow. He said, *Wait here, both of you. I must go up alone and pray.*

“He climbed the hill. Inside the temple it was cool and dark, lit by one lamp before the goddess's image. Dhavala bowed low. And then — in a rush of foolish, fervent devotion — he decided that the greatest gift he had was himself. He took up a sword that lay among the temple offerings and ended his own life before the goddess.”

Vikram's step faltered, just slightly.

“Yes,” said the Betaal, more quietly. “It is a terrible thing, and the story does not praise it. Listen.

“The brother waited. And waited. At last he said to his sister, *I'll go and fetch him.* He climbed the hill, entered the temple, and saw what had happened. Grief and shock overwhelmed him. Thinking he could not face his sister with such news, he too fell before the goddess, and did the same.”

“Madanasundari waited alone at the foot of the hill until the shadows grew long and the birds began going home. Neither her husband nor her brother came back.

“At last, frightened, she climbed up herself. She stepped into the temple — and saw them both lying there, before the goddess, the sword between them.

“She screamed. She wept until she had no tears. And then, beside herself, she too reached for the sword. *What life is there for me now?* she cried.

“But before her hand could close on it, a voice filled the temple — vast, calm, a little exasperated, like a mother whose children have broken every pot in the kitchen. The goddess herself spoke.

“*Stop, child. Enough! Your devotion is real, though theirs was badly judged. I will give them back to you. Put each head back on its body, and they will live.*

“Trembling with joy and terror and haste, in the dim light of a single lamp, Madanasundari did as she was told. She lifted each head and set it on a body. The goddess's power flowed through the temple like warm wind. The two men opened their eyes, breathed, and sat up.”

The Betaal paused, savouring it.

“And then she saw what she had done.”

“In her hurry, she had put her husband's head on her brother's body, and her brother's head on her husband's body.

“The two men looked at each other. Then down at themselves. Then at her. Each had the face he knew and the hands of a stranger.

“*Sister,* said the man with her brother's face. *Wife,* said the man with her husband's face. And both stepped toward her at once.

“They walked down the hill together in silence — the strangest family that ever walked a road. And by the time they reached the village, they were arguing. The one with Dhavala's head said, *I am her husband. This is my face, my mind, my memories of our wedding.* The other, with Dhavala's body, said, *But these are the hands that held hers by the sacred fire. This is the body she married.*

“Madanasundari stood between them and did not know whom to go home with.”

The road had begun to climb. Ahead, very faintly, Vikram could see the glow of the ascetic's fire.

“So, King,” said the Betaal, and its cold breath stirred the king's hair. “Wise Vikram. Just Vikram. Tell me: *which of the two is her husband?*”

Vikram walked on for ten steps. Then twenty. The Betaal waited, humming.

The king knew the rule. He knew that if he spoke, the long walk would be wasted. He also knew that he had an answer — and that to swallow a true answer to save himself effort was not the kind of king he had chosen to be.

“The one with her husband's head,” said Vikram.

“Oh?” said the Betaal. “Why?”

“Because the head is the chief of the body,” said the king. “The scriptures name it first among the limbs. The head holds the mind, the memory, the knowledge of who one is and what one has promised. A man's hands may change; if his mind remains, he remains. The one with Dhavala's head remembers marrying her. He is her husband. The other is her brother, who must learn to live in a new body — and should be honoured for following his sister's husband even into death.”

There was a long silence.

“A good answer,” said the Betaal, quite seriously. “Not the only possible one. But a good one.”

And then, with a whoop of delight, it slid off the king's shoulder and flew like a pale scrap of cloth back across the burning-ground to the peepal tree, where it hung itself up again, swaying, and laughed and laughed.

Vikram stood on the dark road for a moment, looking back.

He was not angry. Kings who lose their tempers at riddles do not make good kings. He simply turned, sheathed his sword, and walked all the way back between the embers, past the river, to the tree.

He climbed. He cut the rope. The body fell and laughed. He lifted it onto his shoulder.

“You are a stubborn man,” said the Betaal, sounding pleased.

Vikram said nothing.

“I think,” said the Betaal, “that I shall tell you another story. There is one about four brothers and a lion that you might find instructive. They were very learned. That was rather the problem.”

The king began to walk.

Far ahead, beside his fire, the smiling ascetic waited, and counted the stars, and was patient. He did not know — not yet — that every answer Vikram gave was making the king wiser, and that wisdom, in the end, would matter more than obedience.

But that is the last of the twenty-five tales, and the night is still young.

*A note from the storyteller.*

In Somadeva's Sanskrit and its many descendants, the details of this tale vary. Sometimes the men are a husband and a friend; sometimes the goddess is named Gauri; sometimes the wife's name is different. Indian storytellers never treated these tales as fixed. They were told on verandas and at fairs and during long train journeys, and each teller added a pause, a joke or a moral of their own.

What stays the same is the shape: a terrible mistake made in haste, a second chance from something greater than us, and a question that cannot be answered by strength or riches — only by thinking.

Try telling it to someone yourself. Stop before Vikram answers, and ask *them*. You may be surprised how fiercely people argue for the body — and how many, when pushed, will say: *She should have asked them who they felt they were.*

That, too, is an answer the Betaal would enjoy.

summary: The Vetala tales are a classic Sanskrit collection, found in Somadeva's 11th-century Kathasaritsagara.
Vikramaditya of Ujjain is a legendary king; historians disagree on whether he was one real ruler.
Frame story: King Vikram must carry a corpse possessed by the Betaal to an ascetic in silence.
Each tale ends in a riddle; if Vikram knows the answer and stays silent his head will burst.
Because he always answers honestly, the Betaal flies back to its tree.
In this tale a husband and brother die at a goddess's temple through rash vows and grief.
The goddess restores them, but the wife places the heads on the wrong bodies.
Riddle: which man is the husband?
Vikram answers: the one with the husband's head, since the head is chief and holds the mind.
A reasoned answer has a claim, reason, evidence, counter-argument and conclusion.
The tale explores identity — mind versus body — and the cost of haste.
Thomas Mann's novella The Transposed Heads (1940) was inspired by this story.

sections.md:
In the first read of this pair, King Vikram carried the Betaal from the peepal tree, heard the tale of the exchanged heads, answered honestly — and lost his prize. He has walked that road many times since.

This read retells, in our own words, two famous parts of the cycle: the tale of **four brothers who bring a lion back to life** (a story also found in the Panchatantra tradition), and the **ending of the whole cycle** — the riddle Vikram cannot answer, and the Betaal's warning about the smiling ascetic.

> Keep asking yourself: is *knowledge* the same as *wisdom*?

sections.md:
Why couldn't the wisest king answer? Let's try. Name the people:

- **Old Father** and his **Son**.
- **Old Mother** and her **Daughter**.
- Old Father marries the **Daughter**. Their child we'll call **A**.
- Son marries the **Old Mother**. Their child we'll call **B**.

Now follow the lines:

1. **Through the fathers.** A's father is Old Father. B's father is the Son — and the Son is Old Father's child, so the Son is A's (half-)brother. The brother of your father is your uncle — so **A is B's uncle**.
2. **Through the mothers.** B's mother is the Old Mother. A's mother is the Daughter — and the Daughter is Old Mother's child, so the Daughter is B's (half-)sister. The brother of your mother is your uncle — so **B is A's uncle**.

Each child is the *uncle* of the other at the same time! Kinship words like *chacha*, *mama*, *bhatija* and *bhanja* assume family trees branch neatly downward. This tree loops back on itself, so the ordinary words break. Vikram saw that every answer led to a contradiction, and he would not pretend to a certainty he did not have.

That is the riddle's real lesson: sometimes the honest answer is *the question does not have one clean answer* — and saying so is wisdom, not weakness.

check.q: In the last riddle, why does Vikram stay silent?
options: He is afraid of the Betaal
The family tree loops so ordinary kinship words contradict each other, and he honestly cannot give one answer
He wants to win the bet
check.why: Because each child is at once the other's uncle, any single relationship word is contradicted, so honest silence is the only true reply.

sections.md:
The lion tale is around a thousand years old in its written forms, but it could be a newspaper headline. Whenever powerful knowledge is used without asking *should we?*, the three scholars are back by the stream.

- **Technology.** Engineers can build apps that keep people scrolling all night. *Can we?* is vidya. *Is it good for the users?* is buddhi.
- **Science.** Doctors and scientists have ethics committees precisely so that a clever experiment is checked by people asking whether it is safe and fair.
- **Everyday life.** Knowing how to bypass a school website's block is a skill; deciding whether to use it is judgement.

Notice too what the story says about the youngest brother. He is laughed at for having 'no science', yet he is the one who finds the water, knows which berries are safe, reads the weather, and — crucially — *listens to his own unease*. Practical knowledge and good sense are a kind of learning that exams don't always measure.

The story is also fair to learning: the three sciences are real marvels. The problem is not knowledge. It is pride — the third brother's 'smallest and proudest smile' — that stops him hearing a warning.
keyTerms: Vidya — formal learning, knowledge
Buddhi — intelligence in the sense of good judgement, discernment
Ethics — thinking about what is right to do, not only what can be done

check.q: Which of these is an example of buddhi rather than vidya?
options: Knowing how to code an app
Deciding not to use a skill because it could harm others
check.why: Buddhi is the judgement to weigh consequences and choose wisely, not simply the possession of knowledge.

sections.md:
- **Vidya vs buddhi.** Learning without judgement can be dangerous — a lesson that rings loud in an age of powerful technology.
- **Honesty as strength.** Vikram's truthfulness costs him time but finally saves his life.
- **Humility.** The wisest moment is admitting *I don't know*.
- **Respect earned.** The Betaal begins as a mocking trickster and ends as an ally — trust built night by night through consistent honesty.

*Did you know?* The Betaal stories inspired Richard Burton's 1870 English adaptation *Vikram and the Vampire*, though it was a loose and heavily embellished version.

check.q: What is the most important lesson Vikram learns at the end?
options: Saying 'I do not know' honestly can be wise
check.why: His honest silence on the unanswerable riddle earns the Betaal's trust and the warning that saves his life.

story.title: The Four Learned Brothers and the Last Riddle

parts.md:
By now King Vikram knew every stone on the path between the peepal tree and the ascetic's fire. He knew where the ground dipped, where the jackals waited, where the river's voice grew loud. He had walked it so many times that his feet had worn a pale line through the ash.

“You are getting thin, King,” remarked the Betaal from his shoulder. “Do they not feed you in Ujjain?”

Vikram said nothing.

“Very well. Tonight's tale is about cleverness. You like cleverness, don't you? Everybody does. Listen.

“In a village in the south there lived four brothers, sons of a poor Brahmin. The eldest three left home young to study at the great centres of learning. They studied for years, under famous teachers, and each mastered a rare and wonderful science. The youngest stayed home and looked after their old parents and the fields. He could read and write, and count the harvest, and tell when the rains would come by the smell of the air. But he had no great learning, and his brothers, when they returned, let him know it.”

“The brothers decided to travel to a rich king's court and win fortunes with their skills.

“*Should we bring him?* asked the eldest, nodding at the youngest. *He has no science. He will embarrass us.*

“*He is our brother,* said the second, a little uncomfortably. *Let him carry the bags.*

“So the youngest carried the bags, and cooked the rice at night, and found the water, and knew which berries were safe and which made you sick. The three scholars talked of nothing but their sciences.

“*I,* said the eldest, *have learned the art of assembling bones. Give me a heap of scattered bones and I can join them into a perfect skeleton.*

“*I,* said the second, *can cover any skeleton with flesh, blood and skin, exactly as it was.*

“*And I,* said the third, with the smallest and proudest smile, *can breathe life back into any body that is whole.*

“The youngest stirred the rice and said nothing. He was thinking that three such sciences, used one after another, could do a very great deal — and that he did not like the look of the forest they were walking into.”

“Deep in that forest, by a dry stream bed, they came upon a heap of bones bleached white by the sun. The skull was huge. The teeth were long.

“The eldest's eyes lit up. *Here is a chance to test our learning before we reach the court!*

“He knelt and began. Bone found bone; joint clicked into joint; the long spine curved; the ribs rose like the timbers of a boat. Within an hour, a perfect skeleton stood on four legs by the stream.

“The youngest set down the bags. *Brother,* he said slowly. *That is the skeleton of a lion.*

“*Obviously,* said the eldest. *A fine specimen.*

“The second brother stepped forward, chanting. Muscles grew like vines over the bones. Skin spread across them, then a tawny coat, then a great dark mane. A lion lay by the stream, whole and perfect, its eyes closed as if sleeping.

“*Brothers,* said the youngest, and his voice was not slow any more. *Please. Stop. If he brings it to life, it will be a living lion. A hungry lion. Lions eat people.*

“The third brother laughed. *You understand nothing of science. This is the greatest test of my art. Do you think I will waste it?*”

“The youngest looked at his three brothers — clever, educated, utterly certain — and at the lion.

“*Then wait,* he said, *just one moment, until I am up that tree.*

“They laughed at him as he scrambled up the tallest tree he could find and clung to a branch high above the ground.

“The third brother closed his eyes, placed his palm on the lion's great forehead, and spoke the words he had learned over twelve long years.

“The lion breathed.

“It opened its golden eyes. It stood. It stretched — and it was very hungry, as anything would be that had been dead a long time.

“The youngest brother, up in the tree, shut his eyes. When he opened them, the lion was walking away into the forest, licking its whiskers, and there was no one left by the stream but him.

“He climbed down when it was safe. He picked up the bags. He went home to his parents, and he looked after the fields for the rest of his life, and whenever anyone in the village boasted about how clever they were, he told them this story.”

The Betaal stretched, comfortable on the king's shoulder.

“So, King. Which of the four was the greatest fool?

“The eldest, who began it? The second, who saw it was a lion and went on? The third, who gave it life? Or perhaps the youngest — who knew what would happen and did not do more to stop them, but simply saved himself?”

Vikram walked, and thought. The moon slid out from behind a cloud and laid his shadow long on the road.

“The third,” he said.

“Why?”

“The first two did not yet put anyone in danger,” said the king. “A skeleton cannot bite; a lifeless lion cannot hunt. But the third saw clearly what was in front of him, heard his brother's warning, and still gave it breath. His was the last choice, and the only one that could not be undone. Knowledge without judgement is not wisdom. He had the most knowledge, and used the least sense.”

“And the youngest?”

“He warned them plainly. He could not stop three grown men by force. He did the sensible thing.”

“Correct, as usual,” sighed the Betaal, and with a shriek of laughter it shot off the king's shoulder and away to its tree.

Many more nights passed. The Betaal told of a thief who laughed and cried at the moment of his death; of three princes, each more delicate than the last; of a girl who brought her own father back to life by sheer argument. Vikram answered every riddle. Every time, the Betaal flew.

And then, one night near the end, the Betaal told a story so tangled that the king could not unpick it.

It was a tale of a father and son who married a mother and daughter — but the father married the daughter, and the son married the mother. In time each couple had children. “So tell me, King,” said the Betaal, “what relation are those children to each other?”

Vikram walked. He worked it one way: cousins, but also… He worked it the other: uncle, nephew, but also sibling of a step-parent… Every answer led to another answer that contradicted it.

He walked ten steps. Fifty. A hundred.

The Betaal waited.

And for the first time in all those long nights, Vikram said nothing at all — not because he wanted to keep his prize, but because he honestly did not know.

The Betaal was quiet for a long while. Then it laughed — but softly, almost kindly.

“Ah,” it said. “At last. A king who can say *I don't know* with his silence. Do you know how rare that is?

“Listen to me now, Vikram, and not as a game. That smiling ascetic who waits for you by his fire is no holy man. He is a sorcerer who wants to rule the world of spirits. He needs the sacrifice of a great king to gain that power — and you are the king. When you bring him my body, he will perform his rites. Then he will say to you, *Bow down before the goddess, flat on the ground, eight limbs touching the earth.* And when your neck is bare, he will strike.

“So when he asks, say this: *I am a king. I have never bowed in that way. Show me how it is done.* And when he lies down to show you—” The Betaal did not finish. It did not need to.

“Why tell me?” asked Vikram. It was the first question he had asked all night.

“Because you answered honestly every time, even when it cost you,” said the Betaal. “And because tonight you were honest enough to be silent. A man like that should not die for a sorcerer's greed.”

The ascetic's fire leapt high as Vikram set down the body. The sorcerer's smile was very wide. He drew diagrams in the ash, scattered rice and sesame, chanted in a voice that made the jackals fall silent.

At last he turned. “Now, great king. Bow before the goddess. Lie flat, all eight limbs to the earth, and receive her blessing.”

Vikram looked at him steadily. “I am a king,” he said. “I have never bowed in such a way. Show me how it is done.”

For a heartbeat the sorcerer hesitated. Then, impatient — so close to his prize — he flung himself flat on the ground to demonstrate.

Vikram's sword flashed once. The sorcerer's ambitions ended in the ash.

The night changed. The fires burned blue, then gold. Somewhere a conch sounded, though no one blew it. The gods themselves, the old stories say, appeared and offered the king a boon.

Vikram thought of the Betaal, and the long road, and all those stories.

“Let these tales,” he said, “be remembered and told across the land, so that anyone who hears them may learn to think.”

And so they were — on verandas and in schoolrooms, in comic books and on television, in every language India speaks. If you are reading this, the boon is still working.

summary: Four brothers: three highly learned, one with only common sense.
They rebuild a lion from bones — skeleton, then flesh, then life.
The youngest warns them and climbs a tree; the lion kills the three scholars.
Vikram judges the brother who gave life as most foolish: his was the final, irreversible act.
Lesson: vidya (learning) without buddhi (judgement) is dangerous; pride blocks warnings.
Near the end, a riddle of tangled family ties leaves Vikram honestly unable to answer.
In that riddle each child turns out to be the other's uncle, so no single word fits.
His honest silence wins the Betaal's trust.
The Betaal reveals the ascetic is a sorcerer planning to sacrifice the king.
Vikram turns the sorcerer's trick back on him and is offered a boon.
He asks that the stories be told everywhere so people learn to think.
